4) Authors used the Beskok and Karniadakis (BK) unified model to describe the enhanced mass
transfer across these thin films. Based on their CFD simulations implementing the BK model,
theoretical results revealed that due to the submicron thickness and the nanoscale pores, the vapor
flux enhancement was considerably higher than the vapor flux produced by microporous
membranes. However, based on Eq. S3&S4, transmembrane BK flux is directly proportional to
the square of the pore radius. Then they assumed the vapor-pressure enhancement due to the curved
meniscus at the entrance of the superhydrophobic nanosized pores of the thin film, resulting in a
substantial increase in the evaporation driving force according to the Kelvin’s equation. However,
how is influencing the said above flux vs. pore radius proportionality compared to the meniscus
effect, and what about the influence of membrane surface porosity, tortuosity and wetting aptitude
(hydrophobicity) in determining the observed amazing mass transfer effects? In this respect, how
can this result be compared to mass transfer mechanisms described e.g., by the Dusty Gas model
which is conventionally used to describe membrane distillation mechanism and for which the
transmembrane flux increases with the pore size?
The simulation results also reported the drastic effect of the thin-film thickness on the vapor fluxes
when the thickness is increased from 120 nm to 1 μm with the water flux decreasing by a factor of
eight, due to an increase of the mass transfer resistance. However, what about heat conduction
through the membrane as the thickness is decreased, and its effect on the temperature polarization
and the net driving force of the process that are still usual issues in DCMD operation?
Response: Thank you for raising these very important points. Indeed, the translation of physical
observations into tractable mathematical models represents a route to understanding the underlying
phenomena that result in the high permeate fluxes exhibited by the new membrane. Nevertheless,
as no approach can claim universality, we would like to share our philosophy with the reviewer
and the approach undertaken in this investigation. Several modes can potentially contribute to
transport in porous media, namely Knudsen diffusion, molecular diffusion and viscous flow.
Regarding transmembrane vapor transport in MD, much effort has focused on finding the parallel
versus in series combination of these transport modes to explain experimental observations1,2. As
mentioned by the reviewer, further progress led to the introduction of more elaborate approaches
such as the dusty gas model (DGM), which is based on Maxwell-Stephan diffusion equation3.
DGM, which finds its developments in catalysis leads to an additive form of vapor diffusion modes
through stagnant air in pores. Yet, DGM has been proved unable to predict simple diffusion with
a stagnant component4, a fact ignored in MD developments before the shortcoming acknowledged
with the publication of the widely used Knudsen-Molecular-Poiseuille-transition (KMPT) model.
These mechanistic approaches have known limits, yet still offer a mathematical form that can
explain observations within specific ranges of parameters and operating conditions. This is
acceptable, since model universality cannot be achieved. The general approach is to minimize the
error between experimental and calculated values by adjusting unknown parameters. The
parameter that is commonly used for calibration is tortuosity, of which determination has seen no
consensus yet whether experimentally or theoretically5. Adopting this approach, the KMPT model
was first implemented during this investigation with the vapor-pressure enhancement caused by
6
meniscus curvature. As can be seen in Fig. S21, the model is unable to explain the trend of the
permeate flux evolution with temperature. Based on these results, we questioned the ability of the
KMPT model to explain the underlying transport mode for the new membrane. As such, the choice
of Beskok-Karniadakis (BK) model, which is based on an extension of the validity of the Navier-
Stokes equations, is not fortuitous. The model is built using a second order slip condition and the
insertion of a rarefaction coefficient thoroughly calibrated using both experiments and direct
simulation Monte Carlo to cover a large practical range of Knudsen numbers. The major difference
with the KMPT model is that the BK model retains the features of a Poiseuille flow, which is
inherent to the model’s nature as derived from momentum equation, while the KMPT model
reduces to diffusion as the pore radius gets smaller in which case the dependence on process
temperature becomes small6. The reducing effect of the square of the radius as it becomes smaller
in BK is compensated by the increase of the rarefaction coefficient as the Knudsen number
becomes higher and the model reflects the dependence of the experimental flux with temperature.
Additional explanations were added to the manuscript in the “Desalination mechanism”
section, page 14.
The effect of the vapor-enhancement as a function of pore radius based on Kelvin equation is now
provided in Fig. S20 (SI, page 35) for different temperatures and a contact angle of 160°.
The enhancement ranges between 8 and 5 at 20 °C and 60 °C, respectively, for a pore radius of 0.495
nm (new data added to the manuscript, pages 6-7 and SI pages 12-13), which explains the flux
differences between the new membrane and the commercial membranes. As for the effect of the
membrane porosity (4.94%; new data added to the manuscript, page 7 and SI pages 7 and 23)
and tortuosity of which value typically ranges between 1.2-2.2, respectively, their variation could
not explain the significant increase of the permeate fluxes compared to common MD membranes.
Regarding the hydrophobicity, we believe that the new thin film being superhydrophobic favors
the meniscus deformation without wetting, leading to the enhancement of the local vapor pressure.
Regarding the reviewer’s concern about the effect of the membrane thickness and how it is related
to heat conduction, the net driving force and polarization, it is very important to first emphasize
that the current multiscale model is fully coupled. Momentum, heat and mass transfer are solved
in both feed and permeate channels in a conjugate approach including heat convection, heat
conduction and mass transfer across the porous membrane. The heat convection part is embedded
via an equivalent thermal conductivity, which includes the heat transfer that accompanies the
evaporation process. The associated cooling of the feed and heating of the permeate are also taken
into account as bulk source terms at the vicinity of the membrane7. As such, the simulation results
showing the significant effect of film thickness on permeate fluxes include all these interrelated
phenomena. It is established from the literature that the evaporation efficiency is a tradeoff
between less resistance to mass transfer and increased conduction losses when thickness is
decreased. However, the literature pertaining to these interrelated phenomena dealt with common
MD membranes. In this investigation, the thin films are two orders of magnitude thinner with a
pore size between two and three orders of magnitude smaller than those of membranes that are
typically used in MD. Therefore, we believe that a translation of literature results related to the
7
range of optimal thicknesses may not be valid, particularly that theoretical approaches are often
based on the use of either the dusty gas model (DGM) or the Knudsen-Molecular-Poiseuille
Transition (KMPT) model. In our work, the KMPT model could not explain the effect of
temperature on the experimental fluxes, which incited us to use the Beskok-Karniadakis (BK)
unified model. The latter, which was derived from momentum equations with a second order
boundary slip condition, incorporates a correction factor for very high Knudsen numbers calibrated
using direct simulation Monte Carlo and experiments, which was able to capture the experimental
trend. Importantly, the calculations of the permeate flux as a function of the membrane thickness
were in good agreement with the experimental values as reported in Fig.3b of the manuscript.
From the same figure, no optimum thickness is visible as it is likely to require the fabrication of
thinner films, which was not possible due to the short reaction time and film fragility below the
range considered in the investigation. Therefore, we came to conclude that the optimum thickness
for the new thin films might have shifted towards smaller thickness values below 60 nm.
To address the reviewer’s concern, a statement is added to the “Desalination mechanism” of the
manuscript to emphasize on the shift of the thickness optimum towards thicknesses smaller than
60 nm compared to orders of magnitude higher values for common MD membranes.
Modifications were brought to the manuscript accordingly on page 14.

5) How pore sizes of TF membranes have been measured and which are their values?
Response: We would like to thank the reviewer for the insightful comment. To address the
reviewer’s request, we employed grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GI-WAXS) to

6) Considering that Authors defined as “free-standing” their films, why they needed to use the
AAO support for their membranes since the support, even if hydrophilic and with large nominal
pore size, introduces somehow additional resistance to mass transfer?
Response: We agree that the use of a support introduces additional resistance to mass transfer.
However, handling the thin film without support is impractical, as it is extremely challenging to
extract it from the organic-aqueous interface in a free-standing form. To address this, we
specifically selected an AAO support to minimize the impact on mass transfer, owing to its large
straight pores. Providing this mechanical support is essential to maintain the structural integrity of
the thin film, particularly during desalination. This approach ensures the film remains intact and
facilitates easier handling in practical applications. This is similar to the structure of reverse
osmosis (RO) membranes, where an ultrafiltration (UF) membrane provides mechanical support
to the active polyamide (PA) desalination layer.

8) Even if concentration polarization has a reduced influence in MD operations compared to
pressure-driven membrane processes, operation at such high transmembrane flux and relatively
low temperature (25 °C) would generate locally at the feed/membrane interface, a rather high
solute concentration that is expected to induce, first, a reduction in water activity and then salts
nucleation due to high supersaturation. This would affect in both cases transmembrane flux by
means of reduced vapour pressure/driving force for water evaporation and then membrane
permeability due crystals deposition on/in the membrane surface (this effect would be even more
pronounced due to solution evaporation in confined pores, thus clogging the pore). How authors
9
comment on this point considering the performances of their membrane for long time operation
(24 h) in the absence of any anti-scaling feature?
Response: We totally agree that concentration polarization and potential salt nucleation are critical
concerns, especially during long-term operations. With the goal to capture the membrane intrinsic
ability to separate water from the feed, we have chosen in our experiments a membrane area large
enough to produce amounts of water that can be measured with accuracy while requiring a small
desalination cell to minimize the flow path along the membrane. Consistently, the selected flow
rate (0.5 L/min) leads to high crossflow velocity (~30 cm/s), which mitigates both concentration
and temperature polarization, ensuring more stable flux over time. Consequently, this approach
limited the accumulation of solutes near the feed/membrane interface and reduced the risk of
localized crystallization.
However, we acknowledge that the reviewer’s comment is particularly relevant for large-scale MD
applications, where concentration polarization and scaling could become more pronounced due to
increased membrane area and longer flow paths. Indeed, in industrial-scale settings, localized
supersaturation at the membrane’s vicinity could lead to salt deposition, potentially clogging the
pores and reducing membrane permeability over time. To address these concerns, the
incorporation of anti-scaling strategies is essential. Potential solutions include the addition of scale
inhibitors, periodic flushing of the membrane system to remove salt deposits and optimizing
module design to maintain high crossflow velocities while minimizing dead zones. These measures
can help limit crystallization risks and support sustained performance during long-term operations.
It is also worth noting that these challenges are not unique to MD but are shared with pressure-
driven processes such as RO. In fact, some researchers argue that current RO membrane
technology may have reached a performance plateau, where further flux enhancement may not
yield significant economic advantages. Nonetheless, ongoing research in RO continues to explore
advanced materials like carbon nanotubes and graphene membranes to enhance flux, despite
similar challenges of concentration polarization and scaling. Therefore, developing effective
solutions for concentration polarization and scaling is imperative for both MD and RO as we
continue advancing towards ultrahigh-flux membranes.
Obaid et. al. present a class of polyamide thin films with ultrahigh flux in membrane distillation,
outstanding salt (>99.8%) and boron rejection (100%), and low energy consumption. These films
were fabricated via a rapid interfacial polymerization (IP) process, and owing to their super-
hydrophobicity, sub-nanometer pore sizes and ultra low thickness (as low as <100nm), these thin
films showed superb vapor flux during membrane distillation with transmembrane temperature
differences ranging from 5 to 40°C. These performance metrics are superior to most commercial
membranes, as well as other hydrophobic membranes reported previously. In my opinion, this
work does not show novelty in terms of membrane material design and fabrication. But on the
other hand, the resultant thin films exhibit excellent desalination relevant properties that are
unprecedented, and which provide unique advantages compared to existing membranes and at the
same time showed good potential towards scale-up and commercialization. I suggest the following
revisions and clarifications for the authors’ consideration.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their invaluable feedback and thoughtful
assessment of our work. We have carefully addressed all the reviewer’s points in the revised
manuscript, including all the requested specific revisions and clarifications.
Comment#1: The authors fabricated the thin films by IP at a support-free organic/water interface,
followed by transferring the film onto a substrate to make a supported composite membrane
relevant to applications. This free-interface method was developed to ensure that the formation of
the film is not affected by the uncontrollable and localized diffusion of the monomers which may
result in inhomogeneity of the film1,2. In my understanding, the goal of this method is to either
achieve a uniformly-structured and ultra-thin film (i.e., <20nm), or controlled polymerization of
certain molecules. However, I did not see a clear reason, or advantage, of using this method in this
work, as the thickness of the films (~90nm) was still in the range of those produced by supported
IP. Since the free-interface IP method severely harms the scalability of such membranes, I would
like to ask the authors to elaborate more on and provide justification for their choice of fabrication
method, possibly by providing a comparison between the membrane made from free-interface and
support IP procedures in terms of their surface morphology and separation performance.
Response: We acknowledge that the support-free organic/water interface (free-interface IP)
method is typically employed to produce ultra-thin and smooth films, benefiting from the high
heat capacity of water to dissipate the exothermic heat generated during IP, thereby promoting
uniform film formation. However, as mentioned by the reviewer, the choice of the free interface
method is to ensure that the film formation is not affected by uncontrolled mass transfer, which
we believe represents a natural choice as a starting point for the analysis of a new category of thin
films. Nevertheless, as the reviewer’s concern is critical, we extended the study by conducting
additional experiments comparing a new set of membranes fabricated by the free-interface IP
method to another new set fabricated by the support-IP (in-situ IP) method. Specifically, we
fabricated TFC membranes using both approaches on four different substrates, namely a
11
commercial PES substrate with a pore size of 0.2 µm, an AAO substrate, and two lab-prepared
electrospun nanofiber substrates (PVDF and PAN). These substrates were selected to provide a
range of pore structures and wettability, for a better comparison of the effect of the two methods
on final film morphology. Thus, we prepared a total of eight TFC membranes (four using free-
interface IP and four using support-IP), scaling the fabrication area to 100 cm² for all substrates
except AAO, which was limited to a 5 cm diameter due to material unavailability. Details of these
experiments are included in a new section of the SI document (Section S8; Pages 42 – 45).
In terms of morphology, SEM analysis (Figs. S24 and S25, pages 43-44) demonstrates that
membranes produced by the support-IP method exhibit a relatively rougher and inhomogeneous
surface structure. This increased roughness is likely due to confinement effects during IP and the
limited ability to dissipate heat generated by the exothermic reaction. In contrast, the free-interface
IP method yielded a smoother film morphology, likely due to water’s thermal dissipation
properties, which mitigates localized heating effects and promotes more uniform film formation.
In order to evaluate the practical impact of these fabrication methods, we assessed the desalination
performance of membranes produced by both techniques (Fig. S26, page 45). Specifically, we
compared the desalination flux and salt rejection of membranes fabricated by free-interface IP and
support-IP on the AAO substrate (Section S8, Fig. S26). Although results show that membranes
prepared by the free-interface IP method give higher permeate fluxes and a better rejection, the
performance of the support-IP membranes is noticeable and remains outstandingly high for a 5 °C
temperature difference as a driving force. Regarding the thickness, the films produced by free-
interface IP were thicker than ultra-thin films typically achievable with this method (such as
polyamide (PA) films). This may be due to the differences in reaction kinetics and the heat
generated in this system, which may differ from those observed during PA films fabrication. We
acknowledge that further studies focusing on the specific reaction kinetics and heat generation in
this system would be beneficial to elucidate these differences. Based on these findings, we totally
agree with the reviewer that for scalability and large-scale applications the support-IP method is
more suitable, despite a slight reduction in flux and rejection compared to free-interface IP. We
have clarified this in the revised manuscript (Pages 17-18) and SI document (Section S8)
with emphasis on the need for a full optimization of the fabrication process to enable translation to an
industrial scale.
Comment#2: The thin films fabricated in this work showed excellent vapor flux when performing
membrane distillation at temperature differences ranging from 5 to 40°C. The performance of the
thin films was superior to that of commercial membranes and recently published membranes. I
have a small comment on the logistics of the membrane testing and comparison: most of the
comparison was done at a transmembrane temperature difference of 5°C, which is not as common
in literatures 3–5. I would like to ask the authors to explain the choice of this condition: is it a
commonly used condition in MD processes when treating certain types of feed solutions, or was
12
this condition chosen to show the maximum difference between the membrane synthesized in this
work and the commercial membranes?.
Response: We would like to thank the reviewer for this thoughtful observation. We totally agree
with the reviewer that most MD studies typically operate at higher transmembrane temperature
differences, often utilizing feed temperatures around 60 °C and permeate temperatures around 20
°C (a 40 °C difference). However, our selection of a lower temperature difference of 5 °C was
intentional and based on two key considerations. Firstly, while higher transmembrane temperature
differences generally increase water flux, they also lead to significantly higher energy demands,
which remains a primary barrier to the broader adoption of MD technology. For instance, studies
conducted at a 40 °C temperature difference report high flux rates, but the associated energy
consumption can exceed 1000 kWh/m³ 1,2,3. By demonstrating strong performance at a lower
temperature gradient, the new thin films offer a more energy-efficient alternative. In our study,
MD performance at feed temperatures as low as 25 °C results in a drastic reduction of the energy
required to run the process, thus enhancing the sustainability and feasibility of MD for large-scale
desalination. Secondly, one of the primary strengths of the new thin films is their ability to sustain
productivity even at minimal temperature differences. This feature is particularly valuable for
applications in regions with limited access to electricity or heating infrastructure, where large
temperature gradients may not be attainable. For example, in desertic regions with ambient
temperatures often above 25 °C, our membrane’s ability to operate effectively at small temperature
differences could enable freshwater production using ambient conditions and minimal external
energy input. This makes MD more accessible for off-grid or low-energy applications, where water
scarcity is often most critical. Furthermore, at large scale application, a multi-stage or multi-effect
concept similar to MSF or MED concepts is necessary to attain high efficiency4-6.

Regarding the degree of crosslinking and its impact on vapor transport, the out-of-plane GI-WAXS

Following the reviewer’s suggestion in the first comment, we have explored the feasibility of a

with the established fabrication processes used for PA layers in commercial TFC-RO membranes,

research is needed to fully optimize this fabrication process and confirm its cost-effectiveness on

production costs while maintaining membrane performance.

fabrication costs, they face notable performance limitations, particularly at low temperatures.
Operating MD at higher temperature differences may increase flux; however, it also introduces
scalability challenges (see previous comments). Specifically, as membrane area increases,
temperature gradients across the membrane are reduced due to polarization, which diminishes the
effective driving force and increases the specific energy consumption. These factors contribute to
higher operational costs for large-scale applications of PTFE membranes in MD.

Comment#6: The authors examined the change in membrane surface morphology with different
IP recipes and showed that the size of leaf-like and ridge-and-valley features increased when the
IP time increases. Since the vapor transport mechanism is heavily dependent on size and number
15
of the sub-nanometer pores/voids in the membrane, I would expect to see a greatly improved
performance when the surface roughness (i.e., accessible surface area) increases 6. However, the
membrane with the best performance (TF0.1-1) is the one with relatively smooth surface. I would
like to ask the authors to provide further discussion on this result, probably on the trade-off

Response: We fully agree that in pressure-driven processes, such as RO, increased surface
roughness, featuring more leaf-like and ridge-and-valley structures, can enhance flux by providing
a greater accessible surface area and more voids for water passage, as the applied pressure directly
drives water through the membrane. However, in our process, rather than a direct hydraulic force,
the driving force is a temperature difference between the feed and permeate sides generating a
vapor pressure gradient across the membrane. In this context, a more complex surface structure
(leaf-like) with additional closed voids1 can trap air and increase the vapor path, thus reducing the
effective driving force and increasing resistance to vapor transport.
As the reviewer noted, there is also a trade-off between surface roughness and membrane
thickness. While increased surface roughness theoretically enhances flux by increasing surface
area, the corresponding increase in thickness reduces overall flux by introducing additional
transport resistance. Additionally, as shown by the out-of-plane GI-WAXS profiles (representing
reciprocal space perpendicular to the thin film surface), each film exhibited unique peak positions
at Q⊥ = 0.36 Å−1, 0.55 Å−1, and 0.90 Å−1, corresponding to d-spacing of 1.748 nm, 1.142 nm,
and 0.698 nm, respectively (Figs. S7 and S8). These decreases in d-spacing correlate with
increased film thickness (Table S3) and suggest that increasing the FTCS concentration likely
facilitate additional polymer growth and denser molecular packing.
We have added a detailed discussion in the manuscript to emphasize the balance between surface
area and membrane thickness, as well as the insights from the out-of-plane GI-WAXS results,
and how these factors collectively influence vapor transport efficiency in MD (Page 9 and 10).

The manuscript titled "Scalable thin films for ultrahigh-efficiency brine desalination" by Obaid et
al. describes the development of superhydrophobic thin films for desalination using membrane
distillation, aiming to achieve high efficiency, low energy consumption, and scalability. The key
innovation in the manuscript is the incorporation of fluorinated trichlorosilane monomers with
long hydrophobic tails during interfacial polymerization to manufacture thin-film composite
membranes suitable for membrane distillation.
Methodology: The synthesis of thin films using interfacial polymerization with fluorinated
trichlorosilanes and diamine-based monomers is well-executed. The authors present a
comprehensive material characterization of the thin films, utilizing a wide range of techniques
such as SEM, AFM, Raman spectroscopy, and FTIR to establish their chemical and morphological
properties. However, the membrane distillation characterization of the new membranes is limited
(see major comments below). The scalability of the membranes is well-supported by the successful
fabrication of large-area films (up to 324 cm²) without compromising mechanical strength.
Novelty and Impact: Membrane distillation membranes are typically ultrafiltration membranes
made using phase inversion. The novelty of the work lies in the development of ultrathin
membrane distillation membranes using interfacial polymerization, which is widely used for
reverse osmosis or nanofiltration membrane manufacture. This approach represents a valuable
contribution to the field of membrane science. However, for a broader journal such as Nature
Communications, significant changes are required to strengthen the manuscript before it can be
reconsidered for publication.
The changes must address the following Major Comments:
1. Energy Efficiency Calculations:
All discussion of the energy efficiency calculations needs to be revised to:
a) Explicitly clarify when only electrical energy consumption has been included in energy
efficiency calculations.
The manuscript should make it explicitly clear in both the abstract and main text when only
electrical energy consumption is being considered. This distinction is crucial because it prevents
misunderstanding about the total energy requirements of the process.
b) Include thermal energy consumption more clearly in the main manuscript and not only in the
Supplementary Information.
Thermal energy or heat consumption is critical to the driving force for mass transfer in thermal
desalination processes like membrane distillation and cannot be omitted from the main manuscript
text. The authors currently emphasize low specific energy consumption (SEC) values but focus
primarily on electrical energy consumption (parasitic losses). A comprehensive energy analysis
19
that includes both thermal and electrical energy inputs is essential for accurately assessing the
process's overall energy efficiency and comparing it with other desalination technologies.
Response: We would like to thank the reviewer for the invaluable comment. To address the
reviewer’s comment, we have revised our approach to energy efficiency calculations in the
manuscript to ensure clarity and thoroughness in distinguishing between electrical and thermal
energy consumption.
Originally, we presented the specific energy consumption (SEC) as a total energy value, combining
both electrical (SEC ) and thermal (SEC ) contributions. However, to address the reviewer’s
elec the
concern and prevent any misunderstanding about the process’s total energy requirements, we have
revised the “Energy Savings” section in the main manuscript (Page 16 -17) and Section S7 in the
SI document (Pages 38 – 42) to clarify this distinction. Throughout the revised manuscript, we
use the term “SEC” explicitly to refer to the total specific energy consumption, which now clearly
encompasses both SEC and SEC . Furthermore, we have changed “specific energy
elec the
consumption” in the abstract to “total specific energy consumption”. Whenever only electrical
energy is considered, it is clearly mentioned in the main text as well as the SI document as SEC
elec
to distinguish it from the combined total SEC calculation. We believe that these changes ensure a
comprehensive energy analysis that accurately reflects both the electrical and thermal energy
inputs, facilitating fair comparison with other desalination technologies and providing a clear
assessment of the overall energy efficiency of the process.
2. Use of Exergy Efficiency:
Given that cheap low-temperature heat is key for the calculations presented, the authors should
use exergy efficiency rather than just energy efficiency to gauge process performance. Exergy
efficiency, taking into account the quality of the heat supplied, would provide readers with a more
accurate description of how efficient the various membrane distillation processes are with these
new membranes compared to the existing literature.
By employing exergy analysis, the authors can account for the actual useful work potential of the
thermal energy sources utilized, especially when low-grade heat is considered. This approach
provides a more meaningful metric for evaluating the thermodynamic efficiency of the process
and facilitates a fair comparison with other desalination technologies that might use higher-grade
energy sources.
Response: To address the reviewer’s insightful comment, we proceeded with a detailed exergy
analysis, which can be found in Supplementary Appendix A, with comments provided in the SI
document (Page 42), and in the manuscript (Page 17). Indeed, the analysis provided additional
insight into the new membrane effectiveness, which showed a low exergy destruction when
operating at low temperatures, far outperforming the commercial membrane by two orders of
magnitude. We would like to emphasize again that the flow rate in our study was purposely set to
a high value to minimize polarization and capture the membrane intrinsic behavior. Therefore, it
20
is expected to lower the exergy destruction in an optimized system design. We would like to thank
again the reviewer for the scrutiny and for suggesting the analysis, which we will take to the next
level with the development of a pilot prototype.
3. Membrane Thermal Conductivity:
The authors need to measure the thermal conductivity of the membrane and report this in the
manuscript. Thermal conductivity is a critical performance parameter in membrane distillation
membranes, as it significantly impacts the actual energy efficiency of the process.
A membrane that is thin but has high thermal conductivity can lead to large entropy generation
from uncontrolled transmembrane heat transfer, reducing the process's overall thermal efficiency.
Additionally, the modeling detailed in Section S6 does not consider heat transfer, despite latent
heat transfer during evaporation and condensation being critical in membrane distillation.
Incorporating thermal conductivity measurements and heat transfer modeling will provide a more
accurate assessment of the membrane's performance and its impact on energy consumption.
Response: To address the reviewer’s important comment, we have measured the membrane’s
thermal conductivity using a Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) device. The
measured values have been added to both the main manuscript (Page 7) and the SI document
(Section 2.8, Page 7 and Page 14).
Regarding the modeling strategy used in the investigation, it is a fully coupled approach that
considers the momentum, heat and species transport in the feed and permeate compartments,
coupled to heat and mass transfer across the porous membrane. The heat transfer across the
membrane includes conduction through the membrane-air-water vapor composite structure and
convection of the latent heat as the hot water vapor molecules are transferred from the feed side to
the permeate side of the membrane. Moreover, the heat extracted from the feed and the heat added
to the permeate as water evaporates and condensates, respectively, is included in the calculations.
Analogously, are considered the water loss from the feed across the feed-membrane interface and
the water gain to the permeate across the permeate-membrane interface.
In order to address the reviewer’s concern, these additional explanations were added to the
manuscript in the “Desalination mechanism” section pages 13-14. Moreover, the equations that
govern heat transfer across the membrane have been added to section S6 (Mathematical and
numerical modeling), pages 33-37 of the SI document. Relevant citation has been included to
refer to the detailed momentum, heat and species transport in the bulk1.
References
1- Soukane S, Ghaffour N. Showerhead feed distribution for optimized performance of large-scale
membrane distillation modules. Journal of Membrane Science 2021, 618: 118664.
21
4. Membrane Thickness:
Membrane thickness is a critical parameter in membrane distillation, as the authors’ research
groups and others have shown. Previous studies have demonstrated that reducing membrane
thickness beyond a certain point can have diminishing returns or adverse effects, such as increased
heat transfer leading to reduced thermal efficiency and reduced exergy efficiency (the authors have
shown that potential mechanical instability is not a major issue here).
The authors should discuss the implications of their membrane's ultrathin structure on both mass
transfer and heat transfer. While thinner membranes can reduce mass transfer resistance and
potentially increase flux, they can also lead to higher heat losses due to increased conductive heat
transfer. An analysis of the trade-offs between membrane thickness and thermal efficiency is
necessary to understand the membrane's optimal design parameters.
Response: We totally agree that membrane thickness is a critical parameter in membrane
distillation. Indeed, many studies including those listed herein1,2,3, report the negative and positive
effects of the membrane thickness, particularly as a function of the solution salinity. However, it
is important to note the range of thicknesses that were investigated and the theoretical models used
to seek for optimums. As such, we believe that these studies consolidate the disruptive nature of
the new category of thin films we synthesized. First, thicknesses of the order of a tenth of a micron
were never considered in the literature and second, the permeabilities used in the theoretical
approaches are either set to values that fall within the range of known commercial membranes or
estimated using theoretical models such as the dusty gas model (DGM) or the Knudsen-Molecular-
Poiseuille transition (KMPT) model.
Within the scope of MD, the DGM shortness to explain temperature effects on permeate fluxes led
to the widely used KMPT4. However, it is very interesting to note that a significant flaw of DGM
has been reported earlier, showing the model inability to predict a simple diffusion with a stagnant
component5. Nevertheless, the model has been used as long as it was able to replicate experimental
investigations for MD membranes within specific ranges of operating conditions. In our
investigation, we are facing an outstandingly fast vapor transfer across films that are two orders of
magnitude thinner with pores that are two to three orders of magnitude smaller compared to
commercial MD membranes. Nevertheless, in our quest to understand the transfer mechanism, we
initially used the KMPT model. Beyond the vapor-pressure enhancement, which we believe is
caused by the meniscus curvature, the KMPT model was unable to explain the flux variations with
temperature. We came to conclude that the attempt of using these known models out of the range
of common membrane properties is very likely not valid, which naturally led us to question the
literature results related to the membrane thickness as the optimality range may have shifted with
the new membrane properties. As such, we used the Beskok-Karniadakis (BK) model because it
is based on an extension of the Navier-Stokes momentum equation with a second-order slip
boundary condition further corrected with direct simulation Monte Carlo and experiments to
extend its validity to very high Knudsen numbers, which was able to reflect the flux dependency
on temperature. In our case, as shown in the experimental results of Fig 3b of the manuscript, the
22
observed flux keeps increasing with thinner films. However, films thinner than 60 nm were
practically not possible to make due to the limited reaction time and their fragility. The results of
Fig.3b let us assume that the ultra-fast vapor transport has shifted the optimal range of membrane
thicknesses commonly used up to date to much thinner values.
References
1. Martínez L, Rodríguez-Maroto JM. Membrane thickness reduction effects on direct contact
membrane distillation performance. Journal of Membrane Science 2008, 312(1): 143-156.
2. Wu HY, Wang R, Field RW. Direct contact membrane distillation: An experimental and
analytical investigation of the effect of membrane thickness upon transmembrane flux. Journal of
Membrane Science 2014, 470: 257-265.
3. Eykens L, Hitsov I, De Sitter K, Dotremont C, Pinoy L, Nopens I, et al. Influence of
membrane thickness and process conditions on direct contact membrane distillation at different
salinities. Journal of Membrane Science 2016, 498: 353-364.
4. Ding Z, Ma R, Fane AG. A new model for mass transfer in direct contact membrane
distillation. Desalination 2003, 151(3): 217-227.
5. Kerkhof PJAM. A modified Maxwell-Stefan model for transport through inert membranes: the
binary friction model. The Chemical Engineering Journal and the Biochemical Engineering
Journal 1996, 64(3): 319-343.
5. Membrane Porosity:
Understanding membrane porosity is vital in membrane distillation membranes because it gives
insight into how membrane permeance and thermal conductivity are impacted by (1) the membrane
material and (2) the membrane architecture.
Porosity influences both the mass transfer (permeate flux) and the thermal conduction through the
membrane. High porosity generally enhances mass transfer but may also increase thermal
conduction if not properly managed. The authors should measure and report the membrane's
porosity, and discuss how it affects the membrane's performance, including any trade-offs between
flux and energy efficiency.
Response: We totally agree with the reviewer that the porosity of the conventional MD membrane
with pore size ranging from 100 nm to 1000 nm is an important factor in traditional MD process
as our group, among others, reported it in earlier investigations1. However, this novel class of
membrane with subnanometer pores (0.495 nm), seems to exhibit a different mechanism where
the driving force is significantly enhanced by the meniscus curvature reaching values far beyond
any highly porous membrane can achieve. We believe that these new findings represent a paradigm
shift in membrane design for membrane distillation where focus should be set on
superhydrophobicity, thinness and reduced pore size. Nevertheless, although not reported in the
23
original manuscript, we measured the porosity of the thin film by dividing the volume of
micropores, which was determined using the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) method, by the total
volume of the thin film. The porosity was estimated at approximately 5%. The details are provided
in the SI document (section 2.9 and 3.6) page 7 and page 23, and in the revised manuscript,
page 7.
References
1. Xu J, Singh YB, Amy GL, Ghaffour N. Effect of operating parameters and membrane
characteristics on air gap membrane distillation performance for the treatment of highly saline
water. Journal of Membrane Science 2016, 512: 73-82.
6. Membrane Pore Diameter:
Membrane pore diameter is an important parameter for membrane distillation membranes because
it provides key insight into liquid entry pressures (LEP), which affect operating pressure and
pressure drop limitations. The authors should measure the pore size distribution of their
membranes and report the average pore diameter. Understanding the pore size is crucial for
ensuring that the membrane can prevent liquid intrusion while allowing vapor transport. This
information will also help assess the membrane's suitability for various operating conditions and
its stability during long-term operation.
Response: To address the reviewer’s concern, we characterized the pore sizes by employing
grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GI-WAXS) to analyze the in-plane structure of the
TF membranes. The GI-WAXS in-plane profiles for the three variants (TFC0.1-1, TFC0.1-2, and
TFC0.1-3) demonstrate consistent peaks at 1.27 Å-1, which corresponds to a pore size of 0.495 nm.
This consistent peak across several samples suggests a similar pore size throughout these thin
films. For a comprehensive description of the GI-WAXS method, please refer to the SI document,
Section 2.7, pages 6-7. The results of this analysis are discussed in detail within the main
manuscript (Pages 6-7, Figs 2i-j added) and the SI document (Pages 12-14).
7. Revision of the Title:
The authors need to revise the title to more accurately reflect the content and focus of the
manuscript. There is no mention of either the chemistry being used or that the desalination is being
performed via membrane distillation. Most readers seeing the current title will think of the
fabrication of thin-film composite reverse osmosis membranes, which are already highly scalable.
Making it clear that these are membrane distillation membranes is vital because thin-film
composite reverse osmosis membranes are not new. Furthermore, using terms like “ultrahigh-
efficiency brine desalination” is potentially misleading because the authors have not fully
accounted for thermal energy in their calculations. The process itself is not more energy efficient
compared to reverse osmosis when considering all energy inputs.
reviewer on the importance of the title relevance to the content. We would like to convince the
reviewer to keep “ultrahigh-efficiency” since we provided a detailed revision of the process
energetics. However, we clarify the nature of the thin film as hydrophobic in the revised title. As
discussed above in several comments, membrane distillation has been used in relevant sections in
the revised manuscript and SI document and added to the keywords.
8. Discussion of technoeconomics:
A large part of the value described in the manuscript is based on “free” low-grade heat or low-
temperature heat. If this argument is central to the paper the authors need to have a discussion
about costs and not just energy efficiency. As the authors note water desalination or brine
concentration costs are only partly dependent on energy consumption. Typically, it is possible to
make a separations process more energy efficient by reducing driving forces and increasing
membrane or adsorbent area. Of course in practical applications, membrane area or separations
footprints are limited by cost.
Response: We totally agree with the reviewer that desalination or brine concentration costs are
just partly dependent on energy consumption. However, in our investigation, we emphasized the
new membrane sustainability, which encompasses both energy saving and productivity. At the
lowest temperature difference set with a feed at 25 °C and a distillate at 20 °C, the membrane
exhibited a SEC of 2.5 kWh.m-3 and 4.4 kWh.m-3 for seawater desalination and brine concentration
while delivering a permeate flux of 40 L.m-2.h-1 and 12 L.m-2.h-1, respectively. This level of
productivity is higher than already commercialized spiral wound air gap MD modules, which
exhibit thermal energy consumption ranging between 150 and kWh.m-3 and 425 kWh.m-3 for a
production of 2 L.m-2.h-1 and 4 L.m-2.h-1, respectively1. Similarly, commercially available flat sheet
technology2 showed a specific thermal energy consumption between 300 kWh.m-3 and 700
kWh.m-3 for a productivity not exceeding 7 L.m-2.h-1. Regarding our membrane, with flat sheets
of 70 cm x 30 cm (as depicted in Fig. 1 of this document), a stacking of 10 sheets for instance
(2.1 m2 of total membrane area) would result roughly in a 75 cm x 35 cm x 15 cm compact module
able to produce more than 2 m3 a day, which represents twice the need of a household. We would
like also to stress the fact that our calculations remain based on a single pass scenario and further
reduction of energy requirements will be achieved with optimized parallel/series modules
configurations. To concur with the reviewer’s vision, we are in the process of scaling up our
findings to a higher technology readiness level. The new prototype will be a key step to optimize
the membrane and adjust the equipment to fully capture the performance. We will share our
findings, including the economics, with the scientific community as we progress in our
developments.
1- A. Ruiz-Aguirre, J.A. Andres-Manas, J.M. Fernandez-Sevilla, G. Zaragoza, Comparative
characterization of three commercial spiral-wound membrane distillation modules, Desalination
and Water Treatment, 61 (2017), 152-159.
2- E.Sh. Mohammed, P. Boutikos, E. Mathioulakis, V. Belessiotis, Experimental evaluation of the
performance and energy efficiency of a Vacuum Multi-Effect Membrane Distillation system,
Desalination, 408, 2017, 70-80.
Conclusion:
The manuscript represents a valuable contribution to the field of membrane science by introducing
a novel approach to fabricating superhydrophobic thin films for membrane distillation. However,
significant revisions are necessary to enhance its suitability for publication in a broad journal like
Nature Communications.
By addressing the major comments outlined above, the authors can improve the clarity, accuracy, and impact of their work.
Including comprehensive energy analyses, detailed membrane characterization (thermal conductivity, thickness, porosity,
pore diameter), and a revised title will strengthen the manuscript and provide a more accurate assessment of the
membrane's performance and potential applications.
Recommendation:
I recommend that the authors revise the manuscript to address the points raised before it can be
reconsidered for publication.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The authors have provided an-depth and sometimes detailed point-by-point response to the comments provided by this reviewer.
Regarding comment 1, it is assumed that the authors talk in their manuscript about the membrane distillation process, this was still not mentioned in the title, abstract or introduction.
In comment 2, in reference to accurately estimating permeate flux in such a small cell, this reviewer is aware of potential bias effects that could mask intrinsic membrane properties with a larger test cell. However, despite the polarization effect, a high-performance membrane would still demonstrate significantly better performance than commercial membranes when tested under the same conditions. The authors prepared a membrane with an area of 2100 cm2 and continued to include the word “Scalable” in the title; therefore, experimental results with a scaled membrane cell would be mandatory. To grasp the real advantage of these membranes, it is necessary to have clear proof that reported transmembrane fluxes are not due to an artefact generated by the small size of the testing cell. The authors used a relatively large apparatus with feed and permeate volumes of 1.5 L each, equipped with a 2-digit scale but a 2 cm2 membrane, in experiments lasting 2 hours (normally, in my experience, it takes 1 to 2 hours to reach steady state conditions before starting the experiment). This point is even more crucial considering that the transmembrane flux also affects the calculated SEC and the claimed energy savings for the relevant membranes.
As an additional comment not included in the initial review report, it is suggested that the Authors discuss the environmental sustainability of the membrane preparation method using IP, particularly in the perspective of large-scale production of such membranes for water desalination. IP is generally considered a “dirty” membrane preparation technique due to the use of organic solvents and/or toxic chemicals.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have done a good job of responding to reviewer comments. Additional notes are below for specific comments
• The authors provided sufficient analysis on the comparison between the morphology of membranes fabricated by supported and support-free interfacial polymerization, including high-quality images of the membrane surface and cross-section, and the detailed performance analysis. Notably, despite the performance drop relative to the membranes made at a free interface, supported IP membranes still maintained high rejections and fluxes comparable to those of commercial membranes across a low temperature gradient. The authors also acknowledged the difference between the two fabrication methods in terms of cost and performance, and well elaborated on my concern.
• The authors provided good explanations on the choice of their experimental conditions and made a strong argument on why it is different from some literature. There is also a section comparing the performance of the lab-made and commercial membranes at different transmembrane temperatures, which answers my original question. I would like to ask the authors to put these arguments somewhere in this paper, probably in the experimental section or the discussion where the specific temperature condition was mentioned, to avoid potential confusion for the readers.
• The new GIWAXS experiments added to the manuscript provide valuable insight into the membrane chemical and physical structures. However, I would suggest the authors to just report the d-spacing and the spectra collected from the GIWAXS experiment, and try not to link it with the free volume or pore size of the membrane, since sometimes they do not match each other. For example, in polyamide network, the calculated ‘pore size’ from GIWAXS may represent the spacing between two aromatic planes rather than the size of channels for transport. I suggest the authors read the following reference [1] on using x-ray scattering to characterize RO material, as it explains well why we cannot use the d-spacing as a direct proxy of membrane pore size, and refine their discussion in this section.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
I would like to thank the authors for their extensive revisions and for the expanded discussion on exergy efficiency. The improvements made so far are appreciated. However, there are a few important points that I would request be addressed before the manuscript can be reconsidered for publication:
1. Reporting of water recovery ratios with SEC: The authors need to give the water recovery ratio with any SEC numbers quoted (along with the initial feed salinity, which they have already included). For example, in the abstract the authors write “Notably, these films achieve the lowest total specific energy consumption reported to date; 1.88 kWh.m−3 for simulated seawater, 3.47 kWh.m−3 for real seawater, and 4.43 kWh.m−3 for real seawater reverse osmosis desalination brine” but in order to know the amount of separation achieved by this energy input we need to know what the water recovery ratio was (i.e., the transmembrane membrane mass or molar flux multiplied by the membrane area and divided by the feed mass or molar flow rate) in order to gauge whether this energy consumption figure is high or low. Quoting energy consumption based on zero- or low-recovery measurements can mislead the reader, especially when compared with the reverse osmosis values for 50% water recovery later in the paper (“This low SEC is close to the reported minimum theoretical energy required for seawater desalination using a large RO system at 50% recovery, estimated at 1.06 kWh.m−3”, referencing Elimelech & Phillip 2011, #78).
2. Impact of Membrane Density and Porosity on Heat Transfer: The authors report a membrane that is dense, relatively non-porous (~5% porosity), and thin. Previous studies have shown that, in membrane distillation, cumulative heat transfer is one of the major challenges with the membranes developed here. Linking back into Point 1, having a thin, low porosity membrane would mean that cumulatively, over the area of a membrane module, the conductive heat loss from the feed to the permeate side would accumulate, drastically reducing the driving force for further water permeation, limiting the water recovery ratio available. The authors should discuss or model this.
3. Clarification on Pore Size / Separation Mechanism: the reported pore sizes measured are very small (sub-nanometer), which could suggest that the membrane might operate more like a pervaporation system—where the polymer sieves salt ions—instead of following a conventional membrane distillation process that relies on a water–vapor interface for the water-salt separation? It would be very helpful if the authors could clarify whether the separation mechanism is driven by a phase change or by molecular sieving, and explain how the small pore size influences the transport mechanism.
4. Keeping / demonstrating the Ultra-High Efficiency Claims: For the ultra-high efficiency claim I think the authors need to show what the energy efficiency of the process is in terms of useful energy out (least work of separation for a given feed salinity and water recovery ratio, assuming 100% salt rejection) divided by the total energy input (including both the electricity and heat). I believe for reverse osmosis with efficient pumps and energy recovery devices the energy efficiency is around 30-40%. If the authors want to keep this claim they should use the flux measurements to estimate the membrane permeance (flux per unit transmembrane chemical potential driving force) and then use this as part of a one-dimensional module-scale model to determine the water recovery. It’s hard to claim ultrahigh efficiency based without knowing the water recovery and how this compares to other processes in the space (e.g., reverse osmosis) even though the figures look promising, this needs to be confirmed.
Recommendation:
I am grateful to the authors for the changes that they have made thus far (and I think they strengthen the manuscript quite a bit), and I recommend that the authors revise the manuscript to address the points raised before it can be reconsidered for publication.

address the reviewer’s comment, we added to the manuscript (Page 16) the recovery values
corresponding to a 1 m2 of membrane and a new section on water recovery in the SI document
(Section S7.3 Page 40), which will allow the readers to assess the significance of the membrane
performance.
Moreover, recovery ratios are inherently scale-dependent and are generally improved by adding
stages (membrane area) to the process flow. For example, small-scale RO systems employing a
single element typically achieve 8–10% water recovery (e.g., an 8% recovery was reported for a
2.2 m² RO module2). In contrast, industrial RO systems, which use 6-7 element configurations
(typically 6-8 elements placed in a pressure vessel) and energy efficient recovery devices, can
achieve recovery ratios of 40–50%3. Similarly, while lab-scale MD systems may initially show
recovery ratios in the range of 7–9%4, advanced configurations and multi-stage operations have
demonstrated recovery ratios of 60–80%5. Moreover, in RO processes, increasing the recovery
ratio necessitates a corresponding increase in applied pressure for subsequent stages due to higher
osmotic pressures caused by higher salinities, which leads to a higher energy consumption further
penalizing the SEC. In contrast, the new membrane operates at atmospheric pressure and room
temperature, which means that recovery ratios can be readily increased with additional stages,
potentially exceeding 70% owing to the smaller effect of the stream concentration on the vapor
pressure compared to its significant effect on the osmotic pressure in the case of RO. Using
Antoine’s equation and a correction function of salinity, one can readily verify that when the salt
concentration reaches 10% (~3 times seawater), the vapor pressure is reduced by about 6%
(p /p0 = 0.94); and when the salt concentration reaches 20% (~5 – 6 times seawater)

water water

bench evaluation of seawater desalination by RO shows a permeate flux below 18 LMH7 when the
osmotic pressure increases beyond 30 bars, while the new membrane delivers 40 LMH under

low-porosity membrane could lead to increased conductive heat transfer across its matrix, our
experimental results show an exceptionally low membrane thermal conductivity (0.07 ± 0.02
W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) (Figure S9, SI, Page 14), which helps reducing heat losses considerably and preserve
the temperature gradient necessary for an efficient water vapor transport. Moreover, it is important
to recall that the driving force in our case is higher than that of standard MD membranes owing to
a higher water vapor pressure caused by the nanosized pores, which we expressed using Kelvin’s
equation (Eq S7, Page 33). This enables the membrane to operate effectively at low feed
temperatures (e.g., 25 °C) with a small transmembrane temperature difference (~5 °C), and further
reduces cumulative conductive heat transfer, as conductive heat losses (Q , Eq. S9, Page 34) are
c
proportional to the temperature gradient. We would like to reassure the reviewer that we modeled
a fully coupled approach of CFD and pore-scale calculations. The model considers both convective
and conductive heat transfer modes from feed to permeate across the membrane as detailed in Eqs.
S11 to S13 (section S6 of the SI document, Pages 32-35). The analysis confirms that the
membrane’s low thermal conductivity and vapor-driven mass transfer mechanism effectively
prevent significant heat loss accumulation.
To address the reviewer’s concern, we added in page 14 of the manuscript a statement highlighting
the important contribution of the low thermal conductivity of the thin film in sustaining the driving
force for distillation.

membrane might operate more like a pervaporation system—where the polymer sieves salt ions—
instead of following a conventional membrane distillation process that relies on a water–vapor

the small pore size influences the transport mechanism.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’ comment on this critical point. In our study, we confirm
that the separation mechanism is driven by phase change, rather than molecular sieving or
pervaporation. The membrane is superhydrophobic, which prevents liquid water penetration and
ensures that only vapor-phase transport occurs through the subnanometer pores. This is readily
verified during the experiments by monitoring the conductivity of the distillate stream. Notably,
the membrane was tested for seawater desalination at the same temperature on both sides. While
a concentration gradient prevails in these experiments, no water flux was observed further
confirming that phase change (evaporation/condensation) is the primary mechanism rather than
diffusion or pervaporation (which requires applying vacuum at the permeate side). Regarding
molecular sieving, although the reported pore sizes in the subnanometer range may suggest a
possible molecular sieving mechanism, the zero flux observed in the isothermal desalination
excludes such a mechanism. This conclusion is further reinforced by the agreement between the
vapor flux enhancement due to nanoconfinement as expressed by Kelvin’s equation and the
permeate flux evolution as a function of feed temperature, as discussed in the manuscript. As such,
the modeling results (see Equation S7 and Figure S20 in the SI, Pages 33-34) show that for a
pore size of ~0.495 nm, the vapor pressure enhancement can reach 10x at 20 °C and 6x at 60 °C,
explaining the observed ultrafast vapor transport.

the process is in terms of useful energy out (least work of separation for a given feed salinity and
water recovery ratio, assuming 100% salt rejection) divided by the total energy input (including
both the electricity and heat). I believe for reverse osmosis with efficient pumps and energy
recovery devices the energy efficiency is around 30-40%. If the authors want to keep this claim
they should use the flux measurements to estimate the membrane permeance (flux per unit
transmembrane chemical potential driving force) and then use this as part of a one-dimensional
module-scale model to determine the water recovery. It’s hard to claim ultrahigh efficiency based
without knowing the water recovery and how this compares to other processes in the space (e.g.,
reverse osmosis) even though the figures look promising, this needs to be confirmed.
Response: To address the reviewer’s concern, we have added 3 new sections (Sections 7.3, 7.4,
and 7.5 in the SI, Pages 40-42), discussing water recovery ratio, membrane permeance, and
energy efficiency, respectively.
We have explicitly calculated the energy efficiency as the ratio of the useful energy output (least
work of separation) to the total energy input (SEC, including both electricity and heat). As
suggested by the reviewer, we evaluated the membrane permeance using the flux data and the
corresponding driving force for all tested solutions. The permeance was found one order of
magnitude higher than that of commercial membranes. Using the permeance values in a one-

efficient energy recovery devices. Similarly, while lab-scale MD systems may initially show

salinity solutions. For example, when the salt concentration reaches 10% (~3× seawater
concentration), the vapor pressure reduction is ~6%, and at 20% salt concentration, the reduction
is only ~15%4.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: After several revisions, the authors have provided convincing answers to nearly all of the reviewers' concerns, and the manuscript has now been satisfactorily reviewed.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
I thank the authors for their revisions. The manuscript is stronger and a couple of the issues previously raised have been addressed. However, one key issue tied to two earlier comments is still unclear and needs resolution.
On page 16 the authors write:
“To validate energy savings under scalable conditions, we conducted strongly coupled multiscale CFD-membrane modeling, which revealed negligible temperature polarization at a feed temperature of 25 °C, enabling consistent operation across varying module lengths and flow rates (SI document Fig. 23a). Under these ambient conditions, the TF0.1–1 membrane achieved a total SEC as low as 1.88 kWh.m−3 at a water recovery ratio (WRR) of 44.4% (Fig. 4d and SI document Fig. 24), without requiring external heating and with minimal cooling demand (SI document Figs. 22a).”
These numbers are quoted elsewhere in the paper and perhaps I am missing something but I do not understand how a WRR of 44.4 % with SEC of 1.88 kWh/m3 is feasible at or near ambient in a single-pass configuration. This remains unclear from a first-law energy balances perspective. In single-pass MD without external heat input, the latent heat to evaporate water must come from sensible cooling of the feed. Assuming enthalpy of vaporization is approximately ΔH_v ≈ 2440 kJ/kg at 25 °C and the specific heat capacity c_p ≈ 4.18 kJ/kg, evaporating 44.4 % of the feed requires approximately1080 kJ per kg of feed (2440 kJ/kg × 0.444). Without external heating, recovering 44.4% of the water through membrane distillation would lead to a temperature drop of about 1080 / 4.18 ≈ 258 °C on the feed side to close the energy balance, which is of course not possible. This back of the envelope calculation assumes that the membrane material is a perfect thermal insulator and that there is no heat loss by conduction. (If the flow rate on the permeate side was equal this would lead to a temperature increase of 258 °C on the permeate side, which is impossible too).
Writing the first-law energy balance the other way around, with inlet temperatures of 25 °C (feed) and 20 °C (permeate), the maximum sensible heat energy available is c_p ΔT, so the bound on the single pass recovery is WRR_max ≈ c_p ΔT / ΔH_v. For ΔT = 5 °C, WRR_max ≈ (4.18 kJ kg-1 K-1 × 5 K) / 2440 kJ kg-1 ≈ 0.86 % far below the 44.4 % reported. Even for a larger temperature difference between the feed and the permeate, say 40 °C feed with 20 °C permeate (ΔT = 20 °C), the same bound gives WRR_max ≈ (4.18 × 20) / 2440 ≈ 3.4 % for a single pass with no heat recovery, still far below 44.4 % WRR mentioned. This is not even accounting for the fact that the permeate temperature will increase as it passes through the membrane module so the actual practicable WRR even lower, regardless of how good the membrane is.
Given these energy balances, the authors need to clarify what the heat or energy source is to make the 44.4 % WRR possible if the system is single-pass at "near-ambient conditions", or else correct the SEC or water recovery rate numbers. For example, explicitly highlighting any external or environmental heat input even if it is considered waste or free heat. As written, the 1.88 kWh/m³ at 44.4 % WRR in single-pass ambient operation appears inconsistent with first-law limits unless additional heat was supplied or if there was membrane wetting. But if there was membrane wetting you no longer have water-salt separation and so those values should not be reported.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author)
I would like to thank the authors for their revisions, the improvements made do strengthen the
manuscript, but they also raise some issues that need to be addressed before the manuscript can
be reconsidered for publication:
Response: We would like to thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and invaluable
comments.
1. Regarding my previous comment on Reporting of Water Recovery Ratios with SEC:
The authors need to give the water recovery ratio with any SEC numbers quoted (along with the
initial feed salinity, which they have already included). For example, in the abstract the authors
write “Notably, these films achieve the lowest total specific energy consumption reported to date;
1.88 kWh.m−3 for simulated seawater, 3.47 kWh.m−3 for real seawater, and 4.43 kWh.m−3 for real
seawater reverse osmosis desalination brine” but in order to know the amount of separation
achieved by this energy input we need to know what the water recovery ratio was (i.e., the
transmembrane membrane mass or molar flux multiplied by the membrane area and divided by
the feed mass or molar flow rate) in order to gauge whether this energy consumption figure is high
or low. Quoting energy consumption based on zero- or low-recovery measurements can mislead
the reader, especially when compared with the reverse osmosis values for 50% water recovery
later in the paper (“This low SEC is close to the reported minimum theoretical energy required for
seawater desalination using a large RO system at 50% recovery, estimated at 1.06 kWh.m−3”,
referencing Elimelech & Phillip 2011, #78).
Response: We fully understand the reviewer’s point and totally agree that the statement may
mislead readers. As suggested by the reviewer in the sequel, we calculated the water recovery ratio
of our membranes using a one-dimensional module-scale model for a 1 m2 membrane area. The
recovery ratio was found to be 44.4%, 15.5%, and 13.3% for NaCl, real untreated seawater
(compared to 8% for 2.2 m2 RO membrane for pretreated seawater), and SWRO desalination brine,
respectively, which underscores the potential for high recovery in a multistage configuration. To
address the reviewer’s comment, we added to the manuscript (Page 16) the recovery values
corresponding to a 1 m2 of membrane and a new section on water recovery in the SI document
(Section S7.3 Page 40), which will allow the readers to assess the significance of the membrane
performance.
Moreover, recovery ratios are inherently scale-dependent and are generally improved by adding
stages (membrane area) to the process flow. For example, small-scale RO systems employing a
single element typically achieve 8–10% water recovery (e.g., an 8% recovery was reported for a
2.2 m² RO module2). In contrast, industrial RO systems, which use 6-7 element configurations
(typically 6-8 elements placed in a pressure vessel) and energy efficient recovery devices, can
achieve recovery ratios of 40–50%3. Similarly, while lab-scale MD systems may initially show
recovery ratios in the range of 7–9%4, advanced configurations and multi-stage operations have
demonstrated recovery ratios of 60–80%5. Moreover, in RO processes, increasing the recovery
ratio necessitates a corresponding increase in applied pressure for subsequent stages due to higher
osmotic pressures caused by higher salinities, which leads to a higher energy consumption further
penalizing the SEC. In contrast, the new membrane operates at atmospheric pressure and room
temperature, which means that recovery ratios can be readily increased with additional stages,
potentially exceeding 70% owing to the smaller effect of the stream concentration on the vapor
pressure compared to its significant effect on the osmotic pressure in the case of RO. Using
Antoine’s equation and a correction function of salinity, one can readily verify that when the salt
concentration reaches 10% (~3 times seawater), the vapor pressure is reduced by about 6%
(p /p0 = 0.94); and when the salt concentration reaches 20% (~5 – 6 times seawater)
water water
(p /p0 = 0.85), the vapor pressure is reduced by only 15%6. This shows that for a similar
water water
permeate flux, the new MD membrane can reach as high of a recovery ratio as RO’s. Additionally,
bench evaluation of seawater desalination by RO shows a permeate flux below 18 LMH7 when the
osmotic pressure increases beyond 30 bars, while the new membrane delivers 40 LMH under
atmospheric pressure and room temperature.

(https://doi.org/10.1016/j.desal.2009.06.072)
2. Impact of Membrane Density and Porosity on Heat Transfer:
The authors report a membrane that is dense, relatively non-porous (~5% porosity), and thin.
Previous studies have shown that, in membrane distillation, cumulative heat transfer is one of the
major challenges with the membranes developed here. Linking back into Point 1, having a thin,
low porosity membrane would mean that cumulatively, over the area of a membrane module,
the conductive heat loss from the feed to the permeate side would accumulate, drastically reducing the
driving force for further water permeation, limiting the water recovery ratio available. The authors
should discuss or model this.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. While we acknowledge that a thin,
low-porosity membrane could lead to increased conductive heat transfer across its matrix, our
experimental results show an exceptionally low membrane thermal conductivity (0.07 ± 0.02
W·m⁻¹·K⁻¹) (Figure S9, SI, Page 14), which helps reducing heat losses considerably and preserve
the temperature gradient necessary for an efficient water vapor transport. Moreover, it is important
to recall that the driving force in our case is higher than that of standard MD membranes owing to
a higher water vapor pressure caused by the nanosized pores, which we expressed using Kelvin’s
equation (Eq S7, Page 33). This enables the membrane to operate effectively at low feed
temperatures (e.g., 25 °C) with a small transmembrane temperature difference (~5 °C), and further
reduces cumulative conductive heat transfer, as conductive heat losses (Q , Eq. S9, Page 34) are
c
proportional to the temperature gradient. We would like to reassure the reviewer that we modeled
a fully coupled approach of CFD and pore-scale calculations. The model considers both convective
and conductive heat transfer modes from feed to permeate across the membrane as detailed in Eqs.
S11 to S13 (section S6 of the SI document, Pages 32-35). The analysis confirms that the
membrane’s low thermal conductivity and vapor-driven mass transfer mechanism effectively
prevent significant heat loss accumulation.
To address the reviewer’s concern, we added in page 14 of the manuscript a statement highlighting
the important contribution of the low thermal conductivity of the thin film in sustaining the driving
force for distillation.
3. Clarification on Pore Size / Separation Mechanism:
The reported pore sizes measured are very small (sub-nanometer), which could suggest that the
membrane might operate more like a pervaporation system—where the polymer sieves salt ions—
instead of following a conventional membrane distillation process that relies on a water–vapor
interface for the water-salt separation? It would be very helpful if the authors could clarify whether
the separation mechanism is driven by a phase change or by molecular sieving, and explain how
the small pore size influences the transport mechanism.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’ comment on this critical point. In our study, we confirm
that the separation mechanism is driven by phase change, rather than molecular sieving or
pervaporation. The membrane is superhydrophobic, which prevents liquid water penetration and
ensures that only vapor-phase transport occurs through the subnanometer pores. This is readily
verified during the experiments by monitoring the conductivity of the distillate stream. Notably,
the membrane was tested for seawater desalination at the same temperature on both sides. While
a concentration gradient prevails in these experiments, no water flux was observed further
confirming that phase change (evaporation/condensation) is the primary mechanism rather than
diffusion or pervaporation (which requires applying vacuum at the permeate side). Regarding
molecular sieving, although the reported pore sizes in the subnanometer range may suggest a
possible molecular sieving mechanism, the zero flux observed in the isothermal desalination
excludes such a mechanism. This conclusion is further reinforced by the agreement between the
vapor flux enhancement due to nanoconfinement as expressed by Kelvin’s equation and the
permeate flux evolution as a function of feed temperature, as discussed in the manuscript. As such,
the modeling results (see Equation S7 and Figure S20 in the SI, Pages 33-34) show that for a
pore size of ~0.495 nm, the vapor pressure enhancement can reach 10x at 20 °C and 6x at 60 °C,
explaining the observed ultrafast vapor transport.
4. Keeping / demonstrating the Ultra-High Efficiency Claims:
For the ultra-high efficiency claim I think the authors need to show what the energy efficiency of
the process is in terms of useful energy out (least work of separation for a given feed salinity and
water recovery ratio, assuming 100% salt rejection) divided by the total energy input (including
both the electricity and heat). I believe for reverse osmosis with efficient pumps and energy
recovery devices the energy efficiency is around 30-40%. If the authors want to keep this claim
they should use the flux measurements to estimate the membrane permeance (flux per unit
transmembrane chemical potential driving force) and then use this as part of a one-dimensional
module-scale model to determine the water recovery. It’s hard to claim ultrahigh efficiency based
without knowing the water recovery and how this compares to other processes in the space (e.g.,
reverse osmosis) even though the figures look promising, this needs to be confirmed.
Response: To address the reviewer’s concern, we have added 3 new sections (Sections 7.3, 7.4,
and 7.5 in the SI, Pages 40-42), discussing water recovery ratio, membrane permeance, and
energy efficiency, respectively.
We have explicitly calculated the energy efficiency as the ratio of the useful energy output (least
work of separation) to the total energy input (SEC, including both electricity and heat). As
suggested by the reviewer, we evaluated the membrane permeance using the flux data and the
corresponding driving force for all tested solutions. The permeance was found one order of
magnitude higher than that of commercial membranes. Using the permeance values in a one-
dimensional scale model we calculated, for 1 m2 of our membrane, water recovery ratios of 44.4%,
15.5%, and 13.3% for simulated seawater (30 g/L NaCl), untreated seawater (40.9 g/L) and brine
(74.4 g/L), which leads to energy efficiencies of 58.1%, 29.5%, and 25.0%, respectively.
Remarkably, the 15.5% (1 m2) water recovery of the new membrane using real untreated seawater
is higher than the 8% (2.2 m2) recovery typical of small-scale RO systems (where advanced treated
seawater is used). As it is the case for RO, recovery values can increase at larger scales, further
highlighting the scalability of the new membrane. Indeed, industrial RO systems can achieve
recovery ratios of 40–50%1 using 6-7 element (placed in a pressure vessel) configurations and
efficient energy recovery devices. Similarly, while lab-scale MD systems may initially show
recovery ratios in the range of 7–9%2, advanced configurations and multi-stage operations have
demonstrated recovery ratios of 60–80%3. Additionally, as discussed in our response to comment
#1, an increase in salt concentration in MD has a less pronounced impact on energy consumption
than in RO, which makes the new membrane particularly advantageous for the treatment of high-
salinity solutions. For example, when the salt concentration reaches 10% (~3× seawater
concentration), the vapor pressure reduction is ~6%, and at 20% salt concentration, the reduction
is only ~15%4.
