## Results

Synthesis of polymeric thin films

We synthesized scalable polymeric thin films with various thicknesses (60.6 to 238.5 nm) for desalination using a straightforward, scalable, and controllable IP technique. This IP involves the reaction between 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorododecyltrichlorosilane (FTCS) and MPD at the interface of two immiscible solutions, forming a superhydrophobic thin film (Fig. 1a and Fig. S1). The freshly prepared FTCS/hexane (organic phase) solution was slowly poured into the MPD/deionized (DI) water (aqueous solution). Upon pouring the FTCS/hexane solution, the head (–SiCl3) of FTCS gets closer to the water surface, whereas its hydrophobic tail remains in the organic phase. Once the FTCS/hexane solution spreads, the head group undergoes rapid hydrolysis and aminolysis reactions with water and MPD, respectively, followed by a condensation reaction (Fig. 1a–c), forming a free-standing superhydrophobic thin film with subnanometer pores at the aqueous–organic interface (Fig. S1a), that was then transferred onto a porous support. Further, we explored the effect of the IP reaction time and FTCS concentration on the thickness, physicochemical properties, and performance of the synthesized thin films (Supplementary Notes 1 and 2). For briefness, the thin-film samples are referred to as TFx–y, where x is the FTCS concentration (wt/vol%) and y is the IP reaction time (min), respectively (e.g., TF0.1–0.5; Table S1). The scalability is demonstrated by fabricating a free-standing thin film with an area of 324.0 cm2 (18 cm × 18 cm) (Fig. S1b), without compromising its mechanical strength. As such, owing to its robust mechanical integrity, the scaled-up free-standing thin film was safely transferred to the surface of a porous support (Fig. S1c). To support scalability, the thin film was also synthesized using the support-IP method29.

Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) observations of the thin films transferred onto the substrate (substrate properties in Table S2) demonstrate the integrity of the thin films (Fig. 1d–h). The morphology of the thin films varied with the FTCS concentration and IP reaction time (Fig. S2). For a short IP reaction time (0.5 min), the thin film exhibited a smooth surface with small nodular features. As the reaction time increased (1–3 min), more prominent leaf-like structures developed, creating a distinct ridge-and-valley topography (Fig. 1d–g and Fig. S2). Increasing FTCS concentration further intensified these surface features, resulting in a denser distribution of leaf-like formations (Fig. S2i–l). The two-dimensional (2D) atomic force microscopy (AFM) images (Fig. 2a and Fig. S3) were consistent with the SEM observations. Cross-sectional SEM images of the thin films on 60 µm-thick substrates revealed film thicknesses ranging from 60.6 nm to 238.5 nm, demonstrating a direct correlation with longer IP reaction times and higher FTCS concentrations (Fig. 2b–f; and Fig. S4 and Table S3). AFM profiling of free-standing thin films, transferred onto silicon wafers, further confirmed that thicknesses remained below 250 nm, with a clear trend of increasing thickness with longer IP reaction times and elevated FTCS concentrations (Fig. 2g, h, Fig. S5). Additionally, surface roughness values varied with the IP reaction time or FTCS concentration (Fig. S6 and Table S3).

Structural insights provided by grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GI-WAXS) provide further understanding of molecular orientation and arrangement within the films (Figs. S7 and S8). The in-plane GI-WAXS profiles of films TF0.1–1, TF0.2–1, and TF0.3–1 exhibit consistent peaks around Q|| = 1.27 Å−1, corresponding to a d-spacing of approximately 0.495 nm30–32. This uniform in-plane feature suggests a consistent molecular arrangement, such as π-π stacking of aromatic groups perpendicular to the supporting substrate, an arrangement likely established during the IP process30,31,33. In contrast, the out-of-plane GI-WAXS profiles exhibited distinct peak positions for each sample (Q⊥ = 0.36 Å−1, 0.55 Å−1, and 0.90 Å−1 for TF0.1–1, TF0.2–1, and TF0.3–1, respectively), corresponding to d-spacing of 1.748 nm, 1.142 nm, and 0.698 nm, respectively (Fig. 2i, j and Figs. S7 and S8). These variations reflect differences in molecular packing density along the out-of-plane direction, likely influenced by polymerization kinetics33–39. This anisotropic arrangement, characterized by consistent in-plane alignment and variable out-of-plane packing, suggests that thickness and cross-linking density may influence transport properties, as thicker films with higher structural density could resist vapor transport due to increased structural complexity.

The estimation of the thin film porosity based on the BET method yielded a value of 4.94% (Supplementary Notes 2.9 and 3.6). The thermal conductivity measurements of the polymeric thin films showed a value of 0.07 ± 0.02 W.m−1.K−1 (Fig. S9), highlighting their strong thermal insulation properties, a crucial factor for efficient desalination. The low thermal conductivity, coupled with controlled structural anisotropy, enables these films to minimize heat loss while allowing selective vapor transport. The chemical structure of the polymeric thin films was validated using Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy (Supplementary Note 3.2). The band at 880 cm−1 is assigned to the Si–N stretching mode40–43, confirming that FTCS reacted with MPD via an aminolysis reaction (Fig. 1b and Fig. S10), forming a continuous thin film (Fig. 1b). Additionally, the bands at 1068 cm−1 and 1024 cm−1 are assigned to the Si–O stretching mode of Si–O–Si (Fig. S10), resulting from hydrolysis and condensation of FTCS, respectively. We characterized the degree of cross-linking in the polymeric thin films by observing the relative intensities of Si–N and Si–O–Si peaks, normalized to an internal C–C reference (Supplementary Note 3.2). The increasing peak ratios, correlating with higher FTCS concentrations and extended reaction time, indicate more cross-linking as revealed in the growth of normalized Si–N and Si–O–Si peaks, suggesting a dynamic interplay between aminolysis and condensation in forming the film structure (Fig. S10 and Table S4). Furthermore, Raman spectroscopy supported the FTIR results (Figs. S10 and S11). Complementing the FTIR findings, Energy Dispersive X-ray (EDX) analysis was conducted to further evaluate the chemical composition and stoichiometry. The analysis of the Si to N ratios (elements unique to FTCS and MPD, respectively) confirmed that the FTCS concentration plays a pivotal role in the film composition. The results from these analytical techniques demonstrate the relationship between monomer concentration and the resulting structure of the polymeric thin film (Table S5). Based on these results, the reaction mechanism can be explained as follows: when the FTCS/hexane solution is added to the MPD/DI water solution, highly active –SiCl3 groups are hydrolyzed by water, forming –Si–OH, whereas others react with MPD to form –Si–NH and release HCl as a byproduct, as illustrated in Fig. S12.

Fluorine-based chains on the thin-film surface could produce low surface energy, imparting superhydrophobicity with water contact angle (WCA) values > 160°. Moreover, varying the IP reaction time or FTCS concentration had a negligible effect on the wettability of the thin films (Fig. S14a and Table S2). Importantly, the thin films exhibited superhydrophobicity towards salty water (30 g.L−1 of NaCl) over a wide range of pH values (1.5–12.0) and toward a surfactant-stabilized oil-in-water emulsion (Fig. S14b). As a comparison, the commercial hydrophobic membranes (with different porosities of 39.6% ± 4.7% (Commercial#1) and 48.3% ± 4.3% (Commercial#2) exhibited WCA values < 135°, smaller than those of the fabricated thin films (Supplementary Note 1.1 and Table S2).

Desalination performance

Before performing desalination experiments, the as-synthesized thin films were transferred onto a commercial hydrophilic substrate. The performance of the thin films was evaluated for the desalination of saline water with different concentrations in term of water-vapor flux and salt rejection using membrane distillation (MD) process. These membranes were sandwiched between the feed (saline solution) and distillate (DI water) streams, with the thin film facing the feed solution (Fig. S15). To provide a slight driving force across the membrane, we set the transmembrane temperature difference at a very low value of 5 °C, using a low feed temperature of 25 °C and a distillate temperature of 20 °C.

The vapor flux was notably influenced by the concentration of FTCS, decreasing with higher concentrations, while the impact of IP reaction time was less pronounced (Fig. 3a). As such, despite increased roughness, which typically enhances flux by increasing surface area, a decline in vapor flux was observed with higher FTCS concentrations or extended reaction times (Table S3). This decline can be attributed to a corresponding increase in film thickness (Fig. 3b) and tighter molecular packing, as evidenced by GI-WAXS out-of-plane profiles (Figs. S7 and S8). Specifically, the d-spacing for TF0.1–1 was approximately 2.5 times greater than for TF0.3–1, reflecting increased compact molecular packing34–36. The decrease in d-spacing and increase in film thickness indicated that higher concentrations promote additional polymer growth and denser molecular packing along the out-of-plane direction (Figs. S7 and S8 and Table S3). The tighter molecular packing and increased cross-linking density observed in thicker films are likely to contribute to increased transport resistance, reducing flux. For example, at a 1-minute reaction time, increasing the FTCS concentration from 0.1% to 0.3% resulted in a substantial thickness increase from 97.5 nm to 238.5 nm (Fig. 3b and Table S3). These structural and morphological variations underscore the trade-off between surface roughness, thickness, and molecular packing, explaining why the thinner, smoother membrane (TF0.1-1) achieved the best performance.

The best-performing thin film, TF0.1–1 (0.1 wt.% FTCS, 1 min reaction time), achieved a vapor flux of 40 ± 3 L.m−2.h−1 and salt rejection of ∼99.9% for simulated seawater (30 g.L−1 NaCl), significantly outperforming commercial membranes (Commercial#1 and Commercial#2), which showed almost zero flux under the same conditions (Fig. 3c). The obtained flux is more than double the RO flux reported for treating seawater with a hydraulic pressure of 55 bar44. Furthermore, the TF0.1–1 efficiently removed both monovalent (K+, Na+, and Cl−) and divalent (Mg2+ and SO4 2−) ions from water with a high separation efficiency of 99.9% (Fig. 3d). However, the flux slightly decreased when divalent ions were used, which could be attributed to the magnesium and sulfate ion scaling and different water activities associated with multivalent ions45. Additionally, the excellent desalination performance of TF0.1–1 was sustained at different NaCl concentrations (Fig. 3e), even when the concentration of the salt in the feed was increased to 70 g.L−1 (brine; 31 ± 3 L.m−2.h−1), which cannot be achieved using RO. Interestingly, the as-prepared thin film (TF0.1-1) exhibits excellent performance towards real seawater (Red Sea salinity = 40.98 g/L, Table S6) and real desalination brine (discharge from SWRO commercial plant = 74.4 g/L, Table S6) with average permeate fluxes of 14 ± 1 and 12 ± 1 L.m−2.h−1 and high salt rejections of 99.3 ± 0.3 and 99.0 ± 0.6%, respectively (Fig. 3f) at a feed temperature of 25 °C and atmospheric pressure. Importantly, while our group reported the evidence of boron volatility (ppb level) in MD starting at about 60 °C, this thin film acts as a full barrier to boron (100% rejection in all cases)46. Furthermore, after the long-term desalination of real feeds, the SEM analysis (Fig. S16a, b) of the used thin films revealed that the morphology remains stable even at high cross-flow velocities, demonstrating its superior mechanical integrity. Moreover, the films showed high resistance to chlorine (Fig. S16c), which further enhances stability. This excellent long-term stability in treating real seawater and real SWRO brine (Fig. 3f) and the fabrication of large samples of 324.0 cm2 (Fig. S1b) demonstrate the possibility of scaling up the composite membrane manufacturing process.

We investigated all synthesized thin films over a wide range of feed temperatures (25 °C–60 °C), covering waste heat generated from industrial plants as low-grade heat sources. For all thin films, the vapor flux increased with an increase in feed temperature due to an increase in driving force (vapor-pressure difference; Fig. 4a and Figs. S17 and S18). In addition, Fig. 4a reveals that the TF0.1–1 membrane provided an ultrahigh vapor flux (238.2 ± 17.5 L.m−2.h−1), six times higher than that of the commercial membranes (41 ± 1 and 38 ± 2 L.m−2.h−1) at a transmembrane temperature difference of 40 °C (feed at 60 °C and distillate at 20 °C). Moreover, the flux exhibited by the TF0.1–1 membrane is higher than that reported for other commercial membranes in the literature (Table S7). Additionally, this desalination flux (at a 60 °C feed temperature) is among the highest values reported in the literature for polymeric and inorganic membranes (Fig. 4b). A TF0.1–1 had higher fluxes than other advanced materials with subnanometer pores, including graphene (226.6 L.m−2.h−1 at 70 °C under −800 mbar vacuum)23, nanoporous carbon (221.6 L.m−2.h−1 at 90 °C and under −825 mbar, VMD mode)24, and COFs (220.0 L.m−2.h−1 at 65 °C and under −160 mbar, VMD mode)25. However, the performance of these materials was assessed under vacuum and higher temperatures, requiring additional energy (Fig. 4b and Table S8). Additionally, all thin films exhibited high salt rejection (>99.0%) due to their superhydrophobicity, which prevented liquid penetration (Fig. S18).

Desalination mechanism

The high vapor flux produced by the thin films could be attributed to several factors. First, vapor-pressure enhancement due to the curved meniscus at the entrance of the superhydrophobic subnanometer pores of the thin film results in a substantial increase in the evaporation driving force. This effect is facilitated by the thin film's low thickness and the hydrophobicity gradient provided by the hydrophilic support. By performing additional experiments, we confirmed the hypothesis that the finely tuned properties of the thin film, such as the lower thickness and a lesser degree of cross-linking, represent the main contribution to the high vapor flux. The original hydrophilic substrate and modified hydrophobic substrate (pore size = 0.2 µm) were evaluated in the same desalination system at a high feed temperature of 60 °C. As presented in Fig. S19, the hydrophilic support demonstrated no salt rejection due to its hydrophilicity, as expected. In addition, the modified hydrophobic support produced a very low vapor flux value of 16.8 ± 2 L.m−2.h−1 and 99.99% salt rejection (feed at 60 °C and distillate at 20 °C). However, the membrane did not produce any flux at 25 °C inlet feed. The poor performance of the hydrophobic support confirms that the fabricated thin film is the key to the experimentally observed high desalination performance. Recent molecular dynamics simulations and experimental studies have indicated that the water evaporation flux in nanopores is orders of magnitude higher than that of bulk water evaporation. In addition, the evaporation rate is significantly increased by reducing the confinement characteristic size47,48, which could be useful in designing efficient materials for low-energy desalination processes. Molecular dynamics simulations, conducted at 27 °C and low pressure (≤ 1 atm), revealed that water exists in a vapor-like state in hydrophobic subnanometer carbon nanotubes (0.8–1.0 nm)49 and between hydrophobic nanoscale sheets (d ≤ 0.5 nm)50, owing to the peculiar behavior of water under confinement effects51,52.

We further performed an analytical and numerical investigation of transmembrane mass transfer to provide a physical basis for the high vapor fluxes observed using the as-prepared thin films under ambient operating conditions (detailed explanations are provided in Supplementary Note 6). Because the developed thin films have a submicron thickness and subnanometer pores, we used the Beskok and Karniadakis53 (BK) unified model to determine the mass transfer across these thin films. This unified model is based on the solution of momentum equations using a second-order slip boundary condition to account for the gas slippage and rarefaction effects observed in narrow channels of microstructures54. This approach has been successfully used to describe gas transport in porous media55,56 and nanopores57,58. The transmembrane mass-transfer model was embedded in a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) code to account for the entire desalination system used in these experiments, including feed and distillate channels. This implementation enables the prediction of momentum, heat, and mass transfer in both channels, coupled in a conjugate approach with heat and mass transfer across the thin film59,60. The heat transfer across the membrane includes the conduction across the membrane-air-water vapor composite structure as well as the latent heat transferred with the vapor convection from the feed to the permeate side of the membrane. Additionally, the heat extracted from the feed and added to the permeate as water evaporates and condensates, respectively, is taken into account in the calculations (see equations in Supplementary Note 6). Computations were performed to estimate the theoretical water-vapor flux, in which the effect of vapor-pressure enhancement (water evaporation in hydrophobic nanopores) was considered using the Kelvin equation, which remains valid in nanometer confinements (Fig. S20)61,62. It is worth noting that the Knudsen-Molecular-Poiseuille Transition (KMPT) model, which is a widely used model to describe mass transfer in MD, was not able to reproduce the permeate flux evolution with temperature (see Fig. S21). Given the subnanometer pore size of the prepared membrane, the KMPT model reduces to diffusion, which is less sensitive to temperature changes compared to Poiseuille flow63. On the contrary, the BK model, which retains features of the Poiseuille flow while compensating for the damping of the small pore radius with the rarefaction coefficient, is able to reflect the flux changes with temperature at high Knudsen numbers.

The theoretical results revealed that the vapor flux enhanced by subnanometer pores is considerably higher than the vapor flux produced by common microporous membranes (Fig. 4b, c). The vapor-pressure enhancement occurs primarily on the feed side due to the submicron thickness and subnanometer pores. Indeed, as the moderate flow pressure pushes water at the feed–thin film interface, an increase in local vapor pressure occurs, whereas it remains almost unchanged at the meniscus of the substrate pores because of the larger pore size (~0.2 µm; Fig. 4c).

Moreover, the submicron thickness and the very low thermal conductivity of the thin-film layer play an important role in enhancing the vapor flux by maximizing the driving force across the membrane64. The simulation results reported in Fig. 3b indicate the drastic effect of the thin-film thickness on the vapor fluxes for a feed temperature of 25 °C and a distillate temperature of 20 °C. If the thin-film thickness is increased from 120 nm to 1 µm, which is still considerably thinner than traditional membranes, the water flux decreases by a factor of eight, due to an increase of the mass transfer resistance. The permeate fluxes obtained using the BK model for different thicknesses of the thin films are similar to those in the experimental results (Fig. 3b). Interestingly, in Fig. 3b, there is no apparent optimum in the range of film thicknesses that were fabricated, as the permeate flux keeps increasing with thinner films. Therefore, with an ultrafast vapor transport, a film thickness two orders of magnitude thinner and pore size two to three orders of magnitude smaller than those of common MD membranes, the optimum film thickness below which conduction losses start penalizing the processes has shifted below 60 nm. This is further consolidated with Fig. 4a which demonstrates that the results using the BK model with varying temperatures are aligned with the experimental results (corresponding to the properties of TF0.1–1). The unified model can reproduce the trend of the permeate flux variations, probably due to its calibration at a high Knudsen number using both experiments and simulations53 and its embedding in a fully coupled approach, thus ensuring proper heat and mass transfer from the feed to the permeate domains.

Energy saving

Energy consumption remains a major contributor to the total cost of desalination, making energy efficiency a critical metric for evaluating the membrane performance. We evaluated the specific energy consumption (SEC; kWh.m⁻3) of the fabricated thin-film membrane together with the water recovery ratio (WRRsp)65 in a single pass DCMD configuration (Fig. S22). This comprehensive metric, which accounts for both thermal (SECth) and electrical (SECelec) energy inputs required for the production of distilled water66, includes energy for heating, cooling, and pumping, making it a reliable indicator of system efficiency (see detailed calculations in Supplementary Note 7)67–74.

To validate energy savings under scalable conditions, we conducted strongly coupled multiscale CFD-membrane modeling, which revealed negligible temperature polarization at a feed temperature of 25 °C, enabling consistent operation across varying module lengths and flow rates (Fig. S23a). Under these ambient conditions, the TF0.1–1 membrane achieved a total SEC as low as 1.88 kWh.m−3 with a corresponding single-pass recovery (WRRsp) of 0.32% (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Note 7.2). In this ambient operation, where the feed enters at room temperature without any heating (Fig. S22a), the maximum single-pass water recovery ratio is constrained by the first law of thermodynamics to 0.76% (ΔT=5 oC) (Supplementary Note 7.2). However, since MD is not significantly limited by increasing feed concentration, higher recoveries can be obtained under recirculating operation with auxiliary or waste-heat input using a heat exchanger. When the feed temperature was increased to 35 oC, the SEC increased to 9.37 kWh.m−3 and WRRsp rose to 1.12%. At 40 oC, the SEC reached 12.90 kWh.m−3 with a WRRsp of 1.60%; at 50 oC SEC further increased to 16.65 kWh.m−3 and WRRsp to 2.68%; and at the highest feed temperature of 60 oC, SEC peaked at 20.65 kWh.m−3 with a WRRsp of 3.87%. One can note the one order of magnitude increase in SEC as the temperature is increased from 25 oC to 35 oC, primarily attributed to the substantial thermal energy required to elevate the feed temperature, which intensifies with increasing operating temperatures.

At 60 °C, where the feed was preheated through a heat exchanger followed by external heating (Fig. S22b), the SEC increased more than tenfold compared to ambient operation, reflecting the substantially larger thermal input required and the stronger polarization effects (Fig. S23b). In this configuration, the maximum single-pass recovery is thermodynamically limited at 6.02%. Unlike the ambient case, where higher recoveries can be achieved through recirculation with low-grade heat input, operating at 60 °C inherently requires significant external thermal input, which sharply increases SEC. These findings emphasize the intrinsic advantage of the thin-film membrane in maintaining exceptionally low SEC under near-ambient operation, while providing a clear framework for distinguishing between ambient no-heating operation and high-temperature operation with external thermal input.

Given the membrane low SEC at ambient conditions, we further evaluated SEC across different feed compositions at 25 °C using both synthetic and real feed seawaters (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Note 7). The TF0.1–1 membrane consistently maintains low SEC values across all tested compositions, achieving 2.51 kWh.m⁻3 for 70 g.L⁻1 NaCl (WRRsp of 0.22%), 3.47 kWh.m⁻3 for real untreated seawater (WRRsp of 0.11%), and 4.43 kWh.m⁻3 for real SWRO brine (WRRsp of 0.09%) (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Note 7). Importantly, even when treating challenging high-salinity feeds like SWRO brine, conditions under which RO is generally impractical due to high osmotic pressures, the TF0.1–1 membrane sustains low SECs. The slightly higher SEC observed for real brine (compared to NaCl solutions) is likely due to reduced water flux at elevated salinities, caused by a lower vapor pressure and increased solution complexity. Moreover, the efficacy of MD as an evaporation-based desalination process is commonly assessed via its Gained Output Ratio (GOR). In this context, the fabricated thin film demonstrated an exceptional GOR of 21 (Supplementary Note 7). Additionally, an exergy analysis revealed a low exergy destruction (3.67 kWh.m−3), two orders of magnitude lower than that of a commercial PTFE membrane (>870 kWh.m−3) when operated at the lowest temperature of 25 °C (see detailed analysis in Supplementary Note 9).

For such moderate feed temperatures, if a free heating resource (i.e., waste heat or solar energy) is available, the thermal energy required by the system becomes negligible, and the recovery ratio can be increased beyond the single-pass thermodynamic limit by employing recirculation or multi-effect operation. For example, the discharge (30–40 g.L−1) from the dump condensers of thermal plants at 60 °C or brine discharge (60–70 g.L−1) from thermal desalination processes at approximately 40 °C can be used as feed, significantly reducing the total SEC by offsetting heating demands. In such cases, only the energy needed for pumping or circulating water through the system remains (SECelec), which ranges between 0.1 and 0.4 kWh.m−3 for pilot-scale air gap MD75 and 1.95 kWh.m−3 for a large-scale MD plant76. This low SEC is significantly lower than single-pass DCMD with heat recovery at a 60 °C feed temperature, which exhibits a minimum of 7.7 kWh.m−377.

These results indicate that the fabricated thin films have a high potential for sustainable, energy-efficient desalination in the future. The energy requirements could be reduced to mere fluid recirculation if available heat sources are used, such as low-grade renewable sources (i.e., geothermal and solar energy sources), waste heat, or latent heat from rejected brine. Moreover, using multiple stages, where the latent heat of evaporation is recovered by heating up the inlet feed during vapor condensation in each stage, decreases the SEC value further and drives the system even closer to the thermodynamic limit of the process. This approach enables desalination at low SEC values (Fig. 4d) while maintaining sustainable productivity using a scalable, simple, and low-cost membrane. This performance is combined with the simplicity of the thin-film synthesis process, representing a breakthrough in desalination. This enhanced evaporation process can address water scarcity in arid lands, where solar energy or ambient temperature can be used to operate a system sustainably and obtain sufficient fresh water.

While the thin films demonstrated excellent SEC and desalination performance compared to commercial membranes, it is important to acknowledge that the current fabrication approach, based on a free-interface IP method, may incur higher production costs than those associated with conventional hydrophobic PTFE and SWRO membrane manufacturing. To address scalability and cost concerns, we propose adopting the in-situ IP (support-IP) method, which aligns with the established manufacturing processes used for polyamide (PA) layers in TFC-RO membranes, potentially reducing costs and facilitating large-scale production (see Supplementary Note 8). This method could take advantage of existing industrial infrastructure, enabling a more economical pathway for mass production. As illustrated in Figs. S24 and S25, the free-interface IP method produced a smoother and thinner nanofilm morphology than the support-IP method, likely due to the high heat capacity of water, which dissipates the exothermic heat generated during the IP reaction. In desalination tests (Fig. S26), a slight decrease in flux was observed for thin film fabricated using the support-IP process compared to those made by free-interface IP. Although additional optimization is necessary to ensure cost efficiency at both pilot and industrial scales, we believe this strategy holds promise for the broader economic feasibility of these membranes. Alongside cost and scalability considerations, it is crucial to carefully evaluate the environmental impact of the IP method. Although the large-scale fabrication of the membrane could leverage existing RO membrane manufacturing infrastructure, the conventional IP still involves organic solvents and potentially hazardous chemicals, posing sustainability and environmental safety concerns if not properly managed. Even though industrial-scale RO membrane manufacturing facilities currently adhere to stringent environmental and safety regulations, including solvent recovery systems and rigorous waste disposal protocols, there is an urgent need to pursue eco-friendly alternatives with the development of green solvents and new polymerization techniques aligned with global sustainability objectives.

Furthermore, while commercial PTFE membranes generally offer lower initial fabrication costs, they exhibit significant limitations in terms of productivity at lower operating temperatures, and low-temperature differences such as 5 °C, which restricts their energy efficiency. In contrast, our thin films retain high flux and thus low SEC at minimal temperature differences, offering a more sustainable solution with reduced energy demands. Although further work is required to fully optimize the scalability of this IP-based process, we believe that adopting an in-situ IP approach and aligning the production with TFC-RO infrastructure could significantly reduce costs and environmental impact while preserving the thin films’ high desalination efficiency. This approach, alongside continued design optimization, could enhance the commercial viability of these membranes for sustainable desalination applications.

## Methods

Fabrication of polymeric thin films

For the synthesis of polymeric thin films, free-standing nanoporous hydrophobic polymeric thin films were initially fabricated using the IP technique. In a typical procedure, various amounts (Table S1) of 1H,1H,2H,2H-perfluorododecyltrichlorosilane (FTCS) were dissolved into 30 mL of hexane (Table S2). Similarly, an amount of m-phenylenediamine (MPD) were dissolved in deionized water to make 3 wt./vol.% of MPD/aqueous solution. Then, polymeric thin films were fabricated by carefully layering the hexane solutions FTCS onto the aqueous solution of MPD at room temperature (25 °C), for a selected time (see Table S1 for concentrations and reaction time details for the twelve thin films). Subsequently, the fabricated thin films were removed from the interface and transferred to water, where the low-density thin film remains floating on the surface. The TFC membranes were prepared by simply transferring the floating thins film onto the substrates, followed by curing at 120 °C for 3 min (Fig. 1 and Fig. S1).

Characterization

The surface and cross-sectional morphologies of the supported thin films were investigated using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Nova Nano 630 and FEI Teneo VS). Atomic force microscopy (AFM, Dimension Icon SPM, model Dimension 3100, Veec) was used to measure the topography (2D and 3D) and roughness of the films. The wettability of the thin films was measured using a CAM 200 goniometer (KSV Instruments). Water contact angle (WCA) measurements were performed for at least 10 random positions, and the average value is reported in the results. An attenuated total reflectance Fourier-transform infrared (ATR-FTIR) spectrophotometer (PerkinElmer Spectrum 100S) was used to detect the functional groups present on the surface of the fabricated polymeric thin films. Raman spectroscopy (20-mW power) was used to demonstrate the binding properties of the thin films further. Raman signals were collected using a 473-nm laser system with 50× objective operated at a power of 20 mW. X-ray diffraction spectra (XRD) patterns were obtained using a Bruker D2 PHASER system with CuKα radiation (λ = 1.54178 Å), operating at 40 mA and 40 kV with a step of 0.02°·s−1. Additional details are presented in Supplementary Note 2.

Desalination under ambient conditions

The desalination capabilities of the as-prepared thin films were evaluated at ambient conditions (25 °C) using a variety of saline solutions, including highly brackish water (10 g.L−1), seawater (30 g.L−1), brine (70 g.L−1), and solutions containing various salt ions (MgCl2, KCl, and Na2SO4). Although most MD studies typically operate at higher transmembrane temperature differences, often utilizing feed temperatures around 60 °C and permeate temperatures around 20 °C (a 40 °C difference), we purposely selected a lower temperature difference of 5 °C. Indeed, while a larger temperature gradient generally enhances water flux, it also significantly increases energy demand, which remains a key obstacle to the broader adoption of MD. The prepared membrane demonstrates strong desalination performance under a minimal temperature gradient, thus offering a more energy-efficient alternative.

Desalination tests were conducted in a custom-designed experimental setup (Supplementary Note 4). The desalination performance of these polymeric thin film was quantified by measuring the water-vapor flux (J, L.m−2.h−1) and percentage of salt rejection (SR, %). Water-vapor flux was calculated by dividing the rate of change of the permeate mass by the active membrane area (2 cm2) and water density (Eq. (S1)). Salt rejection was calculated from the conductivity of the feed and permeate as presented in Eq. (S2). Each experiment was replicated at least three times to ensure reproducibility, and the average flux values were reported. All reported measurements were recorded only after the system had reached a stable operating condition.

In addition, the desalination performance of the thin films was tested using actual samples of seawater from the Red Sea and brine from a commercial seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) plant, under ambient conditions (Table S6). The chlorine resistance of the thin films was evaluated by introducing 200 ppm of NaOCl to the feed side during the desalination process; stability and flux measurements were subsequently monitored over a period of three hours. Furthermore, the desalination capabilities under varying thin-film fabrication conditions, specifically the IP reaction time and reactant concentration, were examined. This aspect of the study involved nine different membranes, all assessed at room temperature (25 °C) for their ability to desalinate saline solutions. The performance of these membranes at varied feed temperatures was also investigated to determine the thermal effects on desalination efficiency. Further details can be found in the Supplementary Note 4.

Data availability

The data supporting the findings of this study are available within the article and its Supplementary Information files. All the raw data relevant to the study are available from the corresponding author upon request.

Then they assumed the vapor-pressure enhancement due to the curved meniscus at the entrance of the superhydrophobic nanosized pores of the thin film, resulting in a substantial increase in the evaporation driving force according to the Kelvin’s equation. However, how is influencing the said above flux vs. pore radius proportionality compared to the meniscus effect, and what about the influence of membrane surface porosity, tortuosity and wetting aptitude (hydrophobicity) in determining the observed amazing mass transfer effects? ### Reviewer 3

Methodology: The synthesis of thin films using interfacial polymerization with fluorinated trichlorosilanes and diamine-based monomers is well-executed. The authors present a comprehensive material characterization of the thin films, utilizing a wide range of techniques such as SEM, AFM, Raman spectroscopy, and FTIR to establish their chemical and morphological properties. However, the membrane distillation characterization of the new membranes is limited (see major comments below). The scalability of the membranes is well-supported by the successful fabrication of large-area films (up to 324 cm²) without compromising mechanical strength.
Novelty and Impact: Membrane distillation membranes are typically ultrafiltration membranes made using phase inversion. The novelty of the work lies in the development of ultrathin membrane distillation membranes using interfacial polymerization, which is widely used for reverse osmosis or nanofiltration membrane manufacture. This approach represents a valuable contribution to the field of membrane science. However, for a broader journal such as Nature Communications, significant changes are required to strengthen the manuscript before it can be reconsidered for publication.
The changes must address the following Major Comments:
1. Energy Efficiency Calculations:
All discussion of the energy efficiency calculations needs to be revised to:
a) Explicitly clarify when only electrical energy consumption has been included in energy efficiency calculations.
The manuscript should make it explicitly clear in both the abstract and main text when only electrical energy consumption is being considered. This distinction is crucial because it prevents misunderstanding about the total energy requirements of the process.
b) Include thermal energy consumption more clearly in the main manuscript and not only in the Supplementary Information.
Thermal energy or heat consumption is critical to the driving force for mass transfer in thermal desalination processes like membrane distillation and cannot be omitted from the main manuscript text. The authors currently emphasize low specific energy consumption (SEC) values but focus primarily on electrical energy consumption (parasitic losses). A comprehensive energy analysis that includes both thermal and electrical energy inputs is essential for accurately assessing the process's overall energy efficiency and comparing it with other desalination technologies.
2. Use of Exergy Efficiency:
Given that cheap low-temperature heat is key for the calculations presented, the authors should use exergy efficiency rather than just energy efficiency to gauge process performance. Exergy efficiency, taking into account the quality of the heat supplied, would provide readers with a more accurate description of how efficient the various membrane distillation processes are with these new membranes compared to the existing literature.
By employing exergy analysis, the authors can account for the actual useful work potential of the thermal energy sources utilized, especially when low-grade heat is considered. This approach provides a more meaningful metric for evaluating the thermodynamic efficiency of the process and facilitates a fair comparison with other desalination technologies that might use higher-grade energy sources.
3. Membrane Thermal Conductivity:
The authors need to measure the thermal conductivity of the membrane and report this in the manuscript. Thermal conductivity is a critical performance parameter in membrane distillation membranes, as it significantly impacts the actual energy efficiency of the process.
A membrane that is thin but has high thermal conductivity can lead to large entropy generation from uncontrolled transmembrane heat transfer, reducing the process's overall thermal efficiency. Additionally, the modeling detailed in Section S6 does not consider heat transfer, despite latent heat transfer during evaporation and condensation being critical in membrane distillation. Incorporating thermal conductivity measurements and heat transfer modeling will provide a more accurate assessment of the membrane's performance and its impact on energy consumption.
4. Membrane Thickness:
Membrane thickness is a critical parameter in membrane distillation, as the authors’ research groups and others have shown. Previous studies have demonstrated that reducing membrane thickness beyond a certain point can have diminishing returns or adverse effects, such as increased heat transfer leading to reduced thermal efficiency and reduced exergy efficiency (the authors have shown that potential mechanical instability is not a major issue here).
The authors should discuss the implications of their membrane's ultrathin structure on both mass transfer and heat transfer. While thinner membranes can reduce mass transfer resistance and potentially increase flux, they can also lead to higher heat losses due to increased conductive heat transfer. An analysis of the trade-offs between membrane thickness and thermal efficiency is necessary to understand the membrane's optimal design parameters.
5. Membrane Porosity:
Understanding membrane porosity is vital in membrane distillation membranes because it gives insight into how membrane permeance and thermal conductivity are impacted by (1) the membrane material and (2) the membrane architecture.
Porosity influences both the mass transfer (permeate flux) and the thermal conduction through the membrane. High porosity generally enhances mass transfer but may also increase thermal conduction if not properly managed. The authors should measure and report the membrane's porosity, and discuss how it affects the membrane's performance, including any trade-offs between flux and energy efficiency.
6. Membrane Pore Diameter:
Membrane pore diameter is an important parameter for membrane distillation membranes because it provides key insight into liquid entry pressures (LEP), which affect operating pressure and pressure drop limitations.
The authors should measure the pore size distribution of their membranes and report the average pore diameter. Understanding the pore size is crucial for ensuring that the membrane can prevent liquid intrusion while allowing vapor transport. This information will also help assess the membrane's suitability for various operating conditions and its stability during long-term operation.
7. Revision of the Title:
The authors need to revise the title to more accurately reflect the content and focus of the manuscript. There is no mention of either the chemistry being used or that the desalination is being performed via membrane distillation. Most readers seeing the current title will think of the fabrication of thin-film composite reverse osmosis membranes, which are already highly scalable.
Making it clear that these are membrane distillation membranes is vital because thin-film composite reverse osmosis membranes are not new. Furthermore, using terms like “ultrahigh-efficiency brine desalination” is potentially misleading because the authors have not fully accounted for thermal energy in their calculations. The process itself is not more energy efficient compared to reverse osmosis when considering all energy inputs.
8. Discussion of technoeconomics:
A large part of the value described in the manuscript is based on “free” low-grade heat or low-temperature heat. If this argument is central to the paper the authors need to have a discussion about costs and not just energy efficiency. As the authors note water desalination or brine concentration costs are only partly dependent on energy consumption. Typically, it is possible to make a separations process more energy efficient by reducing driving forces and increasing membrane or adsorbent area. Of course in practical applications, membrane area or separations footprints are limited by cost.

4) Authors used the Beskok and Karniadakis (BK) unified model to describe the enhanced mass
transfer across these thin films. Based on their CFD simulations implementing the BK model,
theoretical results revealed that due to the submicron thickness and the nanoscale pores, the vapor
flux enhancement was considerably higher than the vapor flux produced by microporous
membranes. However, based on Eq. S3&S4, transmembrane BK flux is directly proportional to
the square of the pore radius. Then they assumed the vapor-pressure enhancement due to the curved
meniscus at the entrance of the superhydrophobic nanosized pores of the thin film, resulting in a
substantial increase in the evaporation driving force according to the Kelvin’s equation. However,
how is influencing the said above flux vs. pore radius proportionality compared to the meniscus
effect, and what about the influence of membrane surface porosity, tortuosity and wetting aptitude
(hydrophobicity) in determining the observed amazing mass transfer effects? In this respect, how
can this result be compared to mass transfer mechanisms described e.g., by the Dusty Gas model
which is conventionally used to describe membrane distillation mechanism and for which the
transmembrane flux increases with the pore size?
The simulation results also reported the drastic effect of the thin-film thickness on the vapor fluxes
when the thickness is increased from 120 nm to 1 μm with the water flux decreasing by a factor of
eight, due to an increase of the mass transfer resistance. However, what about heat conduction
through the membrane as the thickness is decreased, and its effect on the temperature polarization
and the net driving force of the process that are still usual issues in DCMD operation?
Response: Thank you for raising these very important points. Indeed, the translation of physical
observations into tractable mathematical models represents a route to understanding the underlying
phenomena that result in the high permeate fluxes exhibited by the new membrane. Nevertheless,
as no approach can claim universality, we would like to share our philosophy with the reviewer
and the approach undertaken in this investigation. Several modes can potentially contribute to
transport in porous media, namely Knudsen diffusion, molecular diffusion and viscous flow.
Regarding transmembrane vapor transport in MD, much effort has focused on finding the parallel
versus in series combination of these transport modes to explain experimental observations1,2. As
mentioned by the reviewer, further progress led to the introduction of more elaborate approaches
such as the dusty gas model (DGM), which is based on Maxwell-Stephan diffusion equation3.
DGM, which finds its developments in catalysis leads to an additive form of vapor diffusion modes
through stagnant air in pores. Yet, DGM has been proved unable to predict simple diffusion with
a stagnant component4, a fact ignored in MD developments before the shortcoming acknowledged
with the publication of the widely used Knudsen-Molecular-Poiseuille-transition (KMPT) model.
These mechanistic approaches have known limits, yet still offer a mathematical form that can
explain observations within specific ranges of parameters and operating conditions. This is
acceptable, since model universality cannot be achieved. The general approach is to minimize the
error between experimental and calculated values by adjusting unknown parameters. The
parameter that is commonly used for calibration is tortuosity, of which determination has seen no
consensus yet whether experimentally or theoretically5. Adopting this approach, the KMPT model
was first implemented during this investigation with the vapor-pressure enhancement caused by
6
meniscus curvature. As can be seen in Fig. S21, the model is unable to explain the trend of the
permeate flux evolution with temperature. Based on these results, we questioned the ability of the
KMPT model to explain the underlying transport mode for the new membrane. As such, the choice
of Beskok-Karniadakis (BK) model, which is based on an extension of the validity of the Navier-
Stokes equations, is not fortuitous. The model is built using a second order slip condition and the
insertion of a rarefaction coefficient thoroughly calibrated using both experiments and direct
simulation Monte Carlo to cover a large practical range of Knudsen numbers. The major difference
with the KMPT model is that the BK model retains the features of a Poiseuille flow, which is
inherent to the model’s nature as derived from momentum equation, while the KMPT model
reduces to diffusion as the pore radius gets smaller in which case the dependence on process
temperature becomes small6. The reducing effect of the square of the radius as it becomes smaller
in BK is compensated by the increase of the rarefaction coefficient as the Knudsen number
becomes higher and the model reflects the dependence of the experimental flux with temperature.
Additional explanations were added to the manuscript in the “Desalination mechanism”
section, page 14.
The effect of the vapor-enhancement as a function of pore radius based on Kelvin equation is now
provided in Fig. S20 (SI, page 35) for different temperatures and a contact angle of 160°.
The enhancement ranges between 8 and 5 at 20 °C and 60 °C, respectively, for a pore radius of 0.495
nm (new data added to the manuscript, pages 6-7 and SI pages 12-13), which explains the flux
differences between the new membrane and the commercial membranes. As for the effect of the
membrane porosity (4.94%; new data added to the manuscript, page 7 and SI pages 7 and 23)
and tortuosity of which value typically ranges between 1.2-2.2, respectively, their variation could
not explain the significant increase of the permeate fluxes compared to common MD membranes.
Regarding the hydrophobicity, we believe that the new thin film being superhydrophobic favors
the meniscus deformation without wetting, leading to the enhancement of the local vapor pressure.
Regarding the reviewer’s concern about the effect of the membrane thickness and how it is related
to heat conduction, the net driving force and polarization, it is very important to first emphasize
that the current multiscale model is fully coupled. Momentum, heat and mass transfer are solved
in both feed and permeate channels in a conjugate approach including heat convection, heat
conduction and mass transfer across the porous membrane. The heat convection part is embedded
via an equivalent thermal conductivity, which includes the heat transfer that accompanies the
evaporation process. The associated cooling of the feed and heating of the permeate are also taken
into account as bulk source terms at the vicinity of the membrane7. As such, the simulation results
showing the significant effect of film thickness on permeate fluxes include all these interrelated
phenomena. It is established from the literature that the evaporation efficiency is a tradeoff
between less resistance to mass transfer and increased conduction losses when thickness is
decreased. However, the literature pertaining to these interrelated phenomena dealt with common
MD membranes. In this investigation, the thin films are two orders of magnitude thinner with a
pore size between two and three orders of magnitude smaller than those of membranes that are
typically used in MD. Therefore, we believe that a translation of literature results related to the
7
range of optimal thicknesses may not be valid, particularly that theoretical approaches are often
based on the use of either the dusty gas model (DGM) or the Knudsen-Molecular-Poiseuille
Transition (KMPT) model. In our work, the KMPT model could not explain the effect of
temperature on the experimental fluxes, which incited us to use the Beskok-Karniadakis (BK)
unified model. The latter, which was derived from momentum equations with a second order
boundary slip condition, incorporates a correction factor for very high Knudsen numbers calibrated
using direct simulation Monte Carlo and experiments, which was able to capture the experimental
trend. Importantly, the calculations of the permeate flux as a function of the membrane thickness
were in good agreement with the experimental values as reported in Fig.3b of the manuscript.
From the same figure, no optimum thickness is visible as it is likely to require the fabrication of
thinner films, which was not possible due to the short reaction time and film fragility below the
range considered in the investigation. Therefore, we came to conclude that the optimum thickness
for the new thin films might have shifted towards smaller thickness values below 60 nm.
To address the reviewer’s concern, a statement is added to the “Desalination mechanism” of the
manuscript to emphasize on the shift of the thickness optimum towards thicknesses smaller than
60 nm compared to orders of magnitude higher values for common MD membranes.
Modifications were brought to the manuscript accordingly on page 14.

6) Considering that Authors defined as “free-standing” their films, why they needed to use the
AAO support for their membranes since the support, even if hydrophilic and with large nominal
pore size, introduces somehow additional resistance to mass transfer?
Response: We agree that the use of a support introduces additional resistance to mass transfer.
However, handling the thin film without support is impractical, as it is extremely challenging to
extract it from the organic-aqueous interface in a free-standing form. To address this, we
specifically selected an AAO support to minimize the impact on mass transfer, owing to its large
straight pores. Providing this mechanical support is essential to maintain the structural integrity of
the thin film, particularly during desalination. This approach ensures the film remains intact and
facilitates easier handling in practical applications. This is similar to the structure of reverse
osmosis (RO) membranes, where an ultrafiltration (UF) membrane provides mechanical support
to the active polyamide (PA) desalination layer.

8) Even if concentration polarization has a reduced influence in MD operations compared to
pressure-driven membrane processes, operation at such high transmembrane flux and relatively
low temperature (25 °C) would generate locally at the feed/membrane interface, a rather high
solute concentration that is expected to induce, first, a reduction in water activity and then salts
nucleation due to high supersaturation. This would affect in both cases transmembrane flux by
means of reduced vapour pressure/driving force for water evaporation and then membrane
permeability due crystals deposition on/in the membrane surface (this effect would be even more
pronounced due to solution evaporation in confined pores, thus clogging the pore). How authors
9
comment on this point considering the performances of their membrane for long time operation
(24 h) in the absence of any anti-scaling feature?
Response: We totally agree that concentration polarization and potential salt nucleation are critical
concerns, especially during long-term operations. With the goal to capture the membrane intrinsic
ability to separate water from the feed, we have chosen in our experiments a membrane area large
enough to produce amounts of water that can be measured with accuracy while requiring a small
desalination cell to minimize the flow path along the membrane. Consistently, the selected flow
rate (0.5 L/min) leads to high crossflow velocity (~30 cm/s), which mitigates both concentration
and temperature polarization, ensuring more stable flux over time. Consequently, this approach
limited the accumulation of solutes near the feed/membrane interface and reduced the risk of
localized crystallization.
However, we acknowledge that the reviewer’s comment is particularly relevant for large-scale MD
applications, where concentration polarization and scaling could become more pronounced due to
increased membrane area and longer flow paths. Indeed, in industrial-scale settings, localized
supersaturation at the membrane’s vicinity could lead to salt deposition, potentially clogging the
pores and reducing membrane permeability over time. To address these concerns, the
incorporation of anti-scaling strategies is essential. Potential solutions include the addition of scale
inhibitors, periodic flushing of the membrane system to remove salt deposits and optimizing
module design to maintain high crossflow velocities while minimizing dead zones. These measures
can help limit crystallization risks and support sustained performance during long-term operations.
It is also worth noting that these challenges are not unique to MD but are shared with pressure-
driven processes such as RO. In fact, some researchers argue that current RO membrane
technology may have reached a performance plateau, where further flux enhancement may not
yield significant economic advantages. Nonetheless, ongoing research in RO continues to explore
advanced materials like carbon nanotubes and graphene membranes to enhance flux, despite
similar challenges of concentration polarization and scaling. Therefore, developing effective
solutions for concentration polarization and scaling is imperative for both MD and RO as we
continue advancing towards ultrahigh-flux membranes.
Obaid et. al. present a class of polyamide thin films with ultrahigh flux in membrane distillation,
outstanding salt (>99.8%) and boron rejection (100%), and low energy consumption. These films
were fabricated via a rapid interfacial polymerization (IP) process, and owing to their super-
hydrophobicity, sub-nanometer pore sizes and ultra low thickness (as low as <100nm), these thin
films showed superb vapor flux during membrane distillation with transmembrane temperature
differences ranging from 5 to 40°C. These performance metrics are superior to most commercial
membranes, as well as other hydrophobic membranes reported previously. In my opinion, this
work does not show novelty in terms of membrane material design and fabrication. But on the
other hand, the resultant thin films exhibit excellent desalination relevant properties that are
unprecedented, and which provide unique advantages compared to existing membranes and at the
same time showed good potential towards scale-up and commercialization. I suggest the following
revisions and clarifications for the authors’ consideration.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their invaluable feedback and thoughtful
assessment of our work. We have carefully addressed all the reviewer’s points in the revised
manuscript, including all the requested specific revisions and clarifications.
Comment#1: The authors fabricated the thin films by IP at a support-free organic/water interface,
followed by transferring the film onto a substrate to make a supported composite membrane
relevant to applications. This free-interface method was developed to ensure that the formation of
the film is not affected by the uncontrollable and localized diffusion of the monomers which may
result in inhomogeneity of the film1,2. In my understanding, the goal of this method is to either
achieve a uniformly-structured and ultra-thin film (i.e., <20nm), or controlled polymerization of
certain molecules. However, I did not see a clear reason, or advantage, of using this method in this
work, as the thickness of the films (~90nm) was still in the range of those produced by supported
IP. Since the free-interface IP method severely harms the scalability of such membranes, I would
like to ask the authors to elaborate more on and provide justification for their choice of fabrication
method, possibly by providing a comparison between the membrane made from free-interface and
support IP procedures in terms of their surface morphology and separation performance.
Response: We acknowledge that the support-free organic/water interface (free-interface IP)
method is typically employed to produce ultra-thin and smooth films, benefiting from the high
heat capacity of water to dissipate the exothermic heat generated during IP, thereby promoting
uniform film formation. However, as mentioned by the reviewer, the choice of the free interface
method is to ensure that the film formation is not affected by uncontrolled mass transfer, which
we believe represents a natural choice as a starting point for the analysis of a new category of thin
films. Nevertheless, as the reviewer’s concern is critical, we extended the study by conducting
additional experiments comparing a new set of membranes fabricated by the free-interface IP
method to another new set fabricated by the support-IP (in-situ IP) method. Specifically, we
fabricated TFC membranes using both approaches on four different substrates, namely a
11
commercial PES substrate with a pore size of 0.2 µm, an AAO substrate, and two lab-prepared
electrospun nanofiber substrates (PVDF and PAN). These substrates were selected to provide a
range of pore structures and wettability, for a better comparison of the effect of the two methods
on final film morphology. Thus, we prepared a total of eight TFC membranes (four using free-
interface IP and four using support-IP), scaling the fabrication area to 100 cm² for all substrates
except AAO, which was limited to a 5 cm diameter due to material unavailability. Details of these
experiments are included in a new section of the SI document (Section S8; Pages 42 – 45).
In terms of morphology, SEM analysis (Figs. S24 and S25, pages 43-44) demonstrates that
membranes produced by the support-IP method exhibit a relatively rougher and inhomogeneous
surface structure. This increased roughness is likely due to confinement effects during IP and the
limited ability to dissipate heat generated by the exothermic reaction. In contrast, the free-interface
IP method yielded a smoother film morphology, likely due to water’s thermal dissipation
properties, which mitigates localized heating effects and promotes more uniform film formation.
In order to evaluate the practical impact of these fabrication methods, we assessed the desalination
performance of membranes produced by both techniques (Fig. S26, page 45). Specifically, we
compared the desalination flux and salt rejection of membranes fabricated by free-interface IP and
support-IP on the AAO substrate (Section S8, Fig. S26). Although results show that membranes
prepared by the free-interface IP method give higher permeate fluxes and a better rejection, the
performance of the support-IP membranes is noticeable and remains outstandingly high for a 5 °C
temperature difference as a driving force. Regarding the thickness, the films produced by free-
interface IP were thicker than ultra-thin films typically achievable with this method (such as
polyamide (PA) films). This may be due to the differences in reaction kinetics and the heat
generated in this system, which may differ from those observed during PA films fabrication. We
acknowledge that further studies focusing on the specific reaction kinetics and heat generation in
this system would be beneficial to elucidate these differences. Based on these findings, we totally
agree with the reviewer that for scalability and large-scale applications the support-IP method is
more suitable, despite a slight reduction in flux and rejection compared to free-interface IP. We
have clarified this in the revised manuscript (Pages 17-18) and SI document (Section S8)
with emphasis on the need for a full optimization of the fabrication process to enable translation to an
industrial scale.
Comment#2: The thin films fabricated in this work showed excellent vapor flux when performing
membrane distillation at temperature differences ranging from 5 to 40°C. The performance of the
thin films was superior to that of commercial membranes and recently published membranes. I
have a small comment on the logistics of the membrane testing and comparison: most of the
comparison was done at a transmembrane temperature difference of 5°C, which is not as common
in literatures 3–5. I would like to ask the authors to explain the choice of this condition: is it a
commonly used condition in MD processes when treating certain types of feed solutions, or was
12
this condition chosen to show the maximum difference between the membrane synthesized in this
work and the commercial membranes?.
Response: We would like to thank the reviewer for this thoughtful observation. We totally agree
with the reviewer that most MD studies typically operate at higher transmembrane temperature
differences, often utilizing feed temperatures around 60 °C and permeate temperatures around 20
°C (a 40 °C difference). However, our selection of a lower temperature difference of 5 °C was
intentional and based on two key considerations. Firstly, while higher transmembrane temperature
differences generally increase water flux, they also lead to significantly higher energy demands,
which remains a primary barrier to the broader adoption of MD technology. For instance, studies
conducted at a 40 °C temperature difference report high flux rates, but the associated energy
consumption can exceed 1000 kWh/m³ 1,2,3. By demonstrating strong performance at a lower
temperature gradient, the new thin films offer a more energy-efficient alternative. In our study,
MD performance at feed temperatures as low as 25 °C results in a drastic reduction of the energy
required to run the process, thus enhancing the sustainability and feasibility of MD for large-scale
desalination. Secondly, one of the primary strengths of the new thin films is their ability to sustain
productivity even at minimal temperature differences. This feature is particularly valuable for
applications in regions with limited access to electricity or heating infrastructure, where large
temperature gradients may not be attainable. For example, in desertic regions with ambient
temperatures often above 25 °C, our membrane’s ability to operate effectively at small temperature
differences could enable freshwater production using ambient conditions and minimal external
energy input. This makes MD more accessible for off-grid or low-energy applications, where water
scarcity is often most critical. Furthermore, at large scale application, a multi-stage or multi-effect
concept similar to MSF or MED concepts is necessary to attain high efficiency4-6.

production costs while maintaining membrane performance.

fabrication costs, they face notable performance limitations, particularly at low temperatures.
Operating MD at higher temperature differences may increase flux; however, it also introduces
scalability challenges (see previous comments). Specifically, as membrane area increases,
temperature gradients across the membrane are reduced due to polarization, which diminishes the
effective driving force and increases the specific energy consumption. These factors contribute to
higher operational costs for large-scale applications of PTFE membranes in MD.

Comment#6: The authors examined the change in membrane surface morphology with different
IP recipes and showed that the size of leaf-like and ridge-and-valley features increased when the
IP time increases. Since the vapor transport mechanism is heavily dependent on size and number
15
of the sub-nanometer pores/voids in the membrane, I would expect to see a greatly improved

Response: We fully agree that in pressure-driven processes, such as RO, increased surface
roughness, featuring more leaf-like and ridge-and-valley structures, can enhance flux by providing
a greater accessible surface area and more voids for water passage, as the applied pressure directly
drives water through the membrane. However, in our process, rather than a direct hydraulic force,
the driving force is a temperature difference between the feed and permeate sides generating a
vapor pressure gradient across the membrane. In this context, a more complex surface structure
(leaf-like) with additional closed voids1 can trap air and increase the vapor path, thus reducing the
effective driving force and increasing resistance to vapor transport.
As the reviewer noted, there is also a trade-off between surface roughness and membrane
thickness. While increased surface roughness theoretically enhances flux by increasing surface
area, the corresponding increase in thickness reduces overall flux by introducing additional
transport resistance. Additionally, as shown by the out-of-plane GI-WAXS profiles (representing
reciprocal space perpendicular to the thin film surface), each film exhibited unique peak positions

and 0.698 nm, respectively (Figs. S7 and S8). These decreases in d-spacing correlate with
increased film thickness (Table S3) and suggest that increasing the FTCS concentration likely
facilitate additional polymer growth and denser molecular packing.
We have added a detailed discussion in the manuscript to emphasize the balance between surface
area and membrane thickness, as well as the insights from the out-of-plane GI-WAXS results,
and how these factors collectively influence vapor transport efficiency in MD (Page 9 and 10).

The manuscript titled "Scalable thin films for ultrahigh-efficiency brine desalination" by Obaid et
al. describes the development of superhydrophobic thin films for desalination using membrane
distillation, aiming to achieve high efficiency, low energy consumption, and scalability. The key
innovation in the manuscript is the incorporation of fluorinated trichlorosilane monomers with
long hydrophobic tails during interfacial polymerization to manufacture thin-film composite
membranes suitable for membrane distillation.
Methodology: The synthesis of thin films using interfacial polymerization with fluorinated
trichlorosilanes and diamine-based monomers is well-executed. The authors present a
comprehensive material characterization of the thin films, utilizing a wide range of techniques
such as SEM, AFM, Raman spectroscopy, and FTIR to establish their chemical and morphological
properties. However, the membrane distillation characterization of the new membranes is limited
(see major comments below). The scalability of the membranes is well-supported by the successful
fabrication of large-area films (up to 324 cm²) without compromising mechanical strength.
Novelty and Impact: Membrane distillation membranes are typically ultrafiltration membranes
made using phase inversion. The novelty of the work lies in the development of ultrathin
membrane distillation membranes using interfacial polymerization, which is widely used for
reverse osmosis or nanofiltration membrane manufacture. This approach represents a valuable
contribution to the field of membrane science. However, for a broader journal such as Nature
Communications, significant changes are required to strengthen the manuscript before it can be
reconsidered for publication.

3. Membrane Thermal Conductivity:
The authors need to measure the thermal conductivity of the membrane and report this in the
manuscript. Thermal conductivity is a critical performance parameter in membrane distillation
membranes, as it significantly impacts the actual energy efficiency of the process.
A membrane that is thin but has high thermal conductivity can lead to large entropy generation
from uncontrolled transmembrane heat transfer, reducing the process's overall thermal efficiency.
Additionally, the modeling detailed in Section S6 does not consider heat transfer, despite latent
heat transfer during evaporation and condensation being critical in membrane distillation.

Regarding the modeling strategy used in the investigation, it is a fully coupled approach that
considers the momentum, heat and species transport in the feed and permeate compartments,
coupled to heat and mass transfer across the porous membrane. The heat transfer across the
membrane includes conduction through the membrane-air-water vapor composite structure and
convection of the latent heat as the hot water vapor molecules are transferred from the feed side to
the permeate side of the membrane. Moreover, the heat extracted from the feed and the heat added
to the permeate as water evaporates and condensates, respectively, is included in the calculations.
Analogously, are considered the water loss from the feed across the feed-membrane interface and
the water gain to the permeate across the permeate-membrane interface.

4. Membrane Thickness:
Membrane thickness is a critical parameter in membrane distillation, as the authors’ research
groups and others have shown. Previous studies have demonstrated that reducing membrane
thickness beyond a certain point can have diminishing returns or adverse effects, such as increased
heat transfer leading to reduced thermal efficiency and reduced exergy efficiency (the authors have
shown that potential mechanical instability is not a major issue here).
The authors should discuss the implications of their membrane's ultrathin structure on both mass
transfer and heat transfer. While thinner membranes can reduce mass transfer resistance and
potentially increase flux, they can also lead to higher heat losses due to increased conductive heat
transfer. An analysis of the trade-offs between membrane thickness and thermal efficiency is
necessary to understand the membrane's optimal design parameters.
Response: We totally agree that membrane thickness is a critical parameter in membrane
distillation. Indeed, many studies including those listed herein1,2,3, report the negative and positive
effects of the membrane thickness, particularly as a function of the solution salinity. However, it
is important to note the range of thicknesses that were investigated and the theoretical models used
to seek for optimums. As such, we believe that these studies consolidate the disruptive nature of
the new category of thin films we synthesized. First, thicknesses of the order of a tenth of a micron
were never considered in the literature and second, the permeabilities used in the theoretical
approaches are either set to values that fall within the range of known commercial membranes or
estimated using theoretical models such as the dusty gas model (DGM) or the Knudsen-Molecular-
Poiseuille transition (KMPT) model.
Within the scope of MD, the DGM shortness to explain temperature effects on permeate fluxes led
to the widely used KMPT4. However, it is very interesting to note that a significant flaw of DGM
has been reported earlier, showing the model inability to predict a simple diffusion with a stagnant
component5. Nevertheless, the model has been used as long as it was able to replicate experimental
investigations for MD membranes within specific ranges of operating conditions. In our
investigation, we are facing an outstandingly fast vapor transfer across films that are two orders of
magnitude thinner with pores that are two to three orders of magnitude smaller compared to
commercial MD membranes. Nevertheless, in our quest to understand the transfer mechanism, we
initially used the KMPT model. Beyond the vapor-pressure enhancement, which we believe is
caused by the meniscus curvature, the KMPT model was unable to explain the flux variations with
temperature. We came to conclude that the attempt of using these known models out of the range
of common membrane properties is very likely not valid, which naturally led us to question the
literature results related to the membrane thickness as the optimality range may have shifted with
the new membrane properties. As such, we used the Beskok-Karniadakis (BK) model because it
is based on an extension of the Navier-Stokes momentum equation with a second-order slip
boundary condition further corrected with direct simulation Monte Carlo and experiments to
extend its validity to very high Knudsen numbers, which was able to reflect the flux dependency
on temperature. In our case, as shown in the experimental results of Fig 3b of the manuscript, the
22
observed flux keeps increasing with thinner films. However, films thinner than 60 nm were
practically not possible to make due to the limited reaction time and their fragility. The results of
Fig.3b let us assume that the ultra-fast vapor transport has shifted the optimal range of membrane
thicknesses commonly used up to date to much thinner values.

insight into how membrane permeance and thermal conductivity are impacted by (1) the membrane
material and (2) the membrane architecture.

conduction if not properly managed. The authors should measure and report the membrane's
porosity, and discuss how it affects the membrane's performance, including any trade-offs between

membrane with subnanometer pores (0.495 nm), seems to exhibit a different mechanism where
the driving force is significantly enhanced by the meniscus curvature reaching values far beyond
any highly porous membrane can achieve. We believe that these new findings represent a paradigm
shift in membrane design for membrane distillation where focus should be set on
superhydrophobicity, thinness and reduced pore size. Nevertheless, although not reported in the
